description:
# Future Directions — Orthogonal families over the coordinate framework

This cycle specialized the coordinate/incidence framework for generalized nets
to the classical square case and established the Euler–MacNeish ceiling: a
family of pairwise-orthogonal reduced Latin squares of order `n` has at most
`n − 1` members, with the ceiling attained at order three. The pivot argument at
the heart of the proof — inspecting only two grid cells — suggests several bold,
testable next steps.

## Conjecture 1 — Reduction is a free normalization

**Statement.** Every family of pairwise-orthogonal Latin squares of order `n` is
equivalent, under independent symbol relabellings of each square, to a family of
*reduced* squares of the same size, and the equivalence preserves orthogonality.
Consequently the `n − 1` ceiling holds for *arbitrary* (not necessarily reduced)
families.

**The key insight is** that orthogonality is invariant under relabelling the
symbol alphabet of each square separately, because it is a statement about the
*fibres* of the coordinate maps rather than about the symbols attached to them;
reduction is just the choice of relabelling that sends the first row to the
identity.

**Why now?** The pivot proof already localizes the whole argument to two cells,
so the only missing ingredient is a clean lemma that relabelling is a symmetry of
the incidence structure — a small, self-contained addition to the framework that
immediately upgrades the ceiling from reduced families to all families.

## Conjecture 2 — The window bound generalizes to nets

**Statement.** For a generalized net with `m` weft classes and `n` warp classes,
the maximum number of pairwise-orthogonal parallel classes that can be adjoined
is controlled by the number of distinct symbols appearing in a *single bounded
window* of the coordinate grid, generalizing the pivot count from a single cell
to an `r × s` block.

**The key insight is** that the pivot obstruction — distinct nonzero symbols in
one column — is the smallest instance of a general phenomenon: orthogonality
forces injectivity of a "local fingerprint" map, and larger windows yield sharper
ceilings for higher-dimensional nets.

**Why now?** The proof here demonstrates that a two-cell window already yields the
sharp classical bound; extending the fingerprint to a block is a natural,
mechanically checkable escalation that has not been isolated before at this level
of generality.

## Conjecture 3 — Tightness is exactly the prime-power spectrum

**Statement.** Within the coordinate framework, a family attaining the full
`n − 1` ceiling exists if and only if there is a coordinate system on the grid
carrying an affine-plane structure of order `n`; combined with the classical
theory this forces `n` to be a prime power (with the known exceptions `n = 6` and
the still-open `n = 10` on the impossibility side).

**The key insight is** that a complete set of `n − 1` MOLS is interchangeable
with a finite affine plane, and the coordinate/reticulation language makes the
plane's parallel classes literally the fibres of the coordinate maps, turning
"tightness" into "existence of a coordinatizing algebra".

**Why now?** With the ceiling and a concrete tight witness both in hand, the
framework is ready to host the equivalence between complete MOLS families and
affine planes, closing the loop between the incidence axioms and classical
design theory.

## Conjecture 4 — Parastrophy acts freely on saturated families

**Statement.** The parastrophy (coordinate-permutation) action introduced for
reticulations restricts to an action on the set of ceiling-saturating families,
and this action is free whenever `n > 2`; in particular the number of saturated
families up to parastrophy is a divisor-controlled fraction of the total count.

**The key insight is** that a saturated family pins down all six coordinate roles
simultaneously, leaving no nontrivial coordinate permutation that fixes it, so the
symmetry group acts without fixed points once the order exceeds the degenerate
case.

**Why now?** The pivot proof exposes exactly which coordinate roles are forced by
saturation, giving a concrete handle on the stabilizer of a family — the first
step toward an orbit count for small orders.
title: This project formalizes, in Lean 4 (Mathlib), the quantitative and logical core

description:
# Future Directions — Avoidance of t-fold sumsets in dense sets

The results established here pin down the *sharp linear* growth of iterated
sumsets and the deterministic avoidance regime it induces. The gap between this
linear barrier and the conjectural logarithmic threshold frames the following
bold, testable conjectures.

## Conjecture 1 — The logarithmic avoidance threshold for t-fold sumsets

For every integer `t ≥ 2` and every fixed `δ ∈ (0,1)` there is a constant
`C = C(t,δ) > 0` such that, for all large `n`, some set `S ⊆ {1, …, n}` with
`|S| ≥ δn` contains no `t`-fold sumset `A₁ + ⋯ + A_t` whose parts all satisfy
`|Aᵢ| ≥ C · (log n / log(1/δ))^{1/(t−1)}`.

The key insight is that the binding obstruction is not the *size* of the sumset
(which the arithmetic-progression extremiser keeps merely linear) but the number
of *distinct* sumset shapes a dense random set can simultaneously swallow; a
second-moment count over shapes, not over tuples, collapses the exponent from
linear to `1/(t−1)`.

Why now? The `t = 2` case has just been settled with an explicit small constant,
and the sharp iterated growth backbone is now available in fully verified form,
so the induction on `t` finally has a rigorous base and a clean structural step
to climb.

## Conjecture 2 — Sharp exponent `1/(t−1)` is optimal

The exponent `1/(t−1)` in Conjecture 1 cannot be lowered: for every `t` there is
a density `δ` and arbitrarily large `n` for which *every* `δn`-dense set contains
some `t`-fold sumset with all parts of size `≥ c · (log n)^{1/(t−1) − o(1)}`.

The key insight is that a nested arithmetic-progression construction realises a
sumset with `t−1` independent "growth directions," so shrinking the exponent
below `1/(t−1)` would force one direction to carry super-logarithmic length,
which a pigeonhole on residues forbids.

Why now? The extremal examples that saturate the linear backbone (dilated
simplices) are exactly the candidates to be perturbed into the logarithmic
regime, and their growth is now understood exactly.

## Conjecture 3 — Density–threshold trade-off is a genuine power law

Define `k*(n, δ, t)` as the least part-size threshold that admits a `δn`-dense
avoiding set. Then `k*(n, δ, t) = Θ((log n)^{1/(t−1)} · (log(1/δ))^{−1/(t−1)})`
uniformly for `δ` bounded away from `0` and `1`.

The key insight is that `log(1/δ)` and `log n` enter only through their ratio,
because both measure "bits of freedom" — one per excluded element, one per
ambient coordinate — so the threshold must be homogeneous of degree `0` in that
pair after the `(t−1)`-th root.

Why now? The linear backbone already exhibits the exact `1/t`-type scaling in the
part count `t`, isolating `t` as the correct root index and making the joint
`(n, δ)` dependence the only remaining unknown.

## Conjecture 4 — Structural rigidity of near-extremal containers

If a `δn`-dense set `S` contains a `t`-fold sumset with parts of size within a
`(1+o(1))` factor of the threshold, then `S` must contain a long arithmetic
progression (of length `n^{Ω(1)}`).

The key insight is that saturating the growth bound forces every summand to be an
arithmetic progression with a common difference, and a dense container of such a
progression inherits its structure — avoidance and rigidity are two faces of the
same extremal equation.

Why now? The equality case of the iterated growth bound is now identified
exactly (arithmetic progressions), turning a qualitative "structure vs.
randomness" heuristic into a precise, checkable rigidity statement.

description:
# Spectral Graph Theory Meets Network Robustness

## Formal results

`Geometry/SpectralNetworkRobustness.lean` proves a precise conditional version of the proposed spectral certificate.

1. **Exact spectral identity.** For a weighted two-node computation graph, the Dirichlet energy is exactly algebraic connectivity times variance in the unique disagreement mode.
2. **Spectral-to-Lipschitz theorem.** If a scalar internal state satisfies
   \[
   \lambda\,|h(x)-h(y)|^2 \le G^2 |x-y|^2,
   \]
   with \(\lambda>0\), then its Lipschitz constant is at most \(G/\sqrt{\lambda}\).
3. **Readout composition.** A readout with Lipschitz constant \(K\) gives an end-to-end bound \(KG/\sqrt{\lambda}\).
4. **Certified radius.** At a point with positive classification margin \(m\), when \(G,K>0\), the positive decision is certified for every perturbation of magnitude strictly below
   \[
   \frac{m\sqrt{\lambda}}{KG}.
   \]

Thus algebraic connectivity contributes a square-root improvement to the certified radius under an explicit spectral state-gain inequality. The theorem does not confuse graph topology with the independent gain and margin assumptions needed to control the represented function.

## Contrarian conjectures disproved

Two stronger, tempting formulations are false.

- **“Connectivity alone gives a positive robustness radius.”** Disproved uniformly: for every proposed radius \(R>0\), the affine score \(f(x)=R/2-x\) has positive score at zero and is 1-Lipschitz, but reaches zero inside that radius. This counterexample works irrespective of the computation graph's connectivity.
- **“Connectivity alone upper-bounds the network Lipschitz constant.”** Disproved uniformly: for every proposed nonnegative bound \(B\), the linear score \(f(x)=(B+1)x\) violates it. Graph topology cannot prevent arbitrarily large parameter scaling.

These disproofs identify the indispensable quantities omitted by the connectivity-only conjectures: a parameter/state gain bound and a positive output margin.

## Computational evidence decision

A separate computational-evidence artifact was not produced because the claims proved here are exact symbolic identities and uniform parametric counterexamples, rather than a finite or asymptotic conjecture inferred from a numerical sequence. The counterexamples cover every positive candidate radius and every nonnegative candidate Lipschitz bound; sampling small cases would be strictly weaker. There is consequently no associated integer sequence or meaningful OEIS query. The two-node spectral calculation is formalized exactly in Lean, avoiding floating-point eigensolver evidence.

## Future directions

1. Replace the scalar `SpectralStateBound` assumption by a theorem derived from a finite graph Laplacian, its Rayleigh quotient, and orthogonality to the constant mode.
2. Generalize scalar inputs, states, and scores to finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces and operator norms.
3. Derive state gain bounds compositionally from layer weight matrices, 1-Lipschitz activations, residual edges, and message-passing operators.
4. Formalize multiclass certification using the gap between the winning logit and every competing logit.
5. Separate normalized and unnormalized Laplacians and track degree dependence in the resulting certificates.
6. Study whether graph rewiring that increases algebraic connectivity can worsen parameter gain enough to reduce the final certified radius; the proved formula shows this tradeoff must be controlled.
7. Extend the deterministic result to node/edge deletion certificates using interlacing bounds for perturbed Laplacians.

# Future Directions

The proposed mixed-area formula needs a normalization correction. For standard degree triangles, normalized lattice area satisfies

\[
A((d+e)\Delta)-A(d\Delta)-A(e\Delta)=2de.
\]

Thus the raw polarization of normalized lattice area is twice the plane Bézout number. In particular, two tropical lines give area difference `2`, while their stable intersection number is `1`. The corrected convention is

\[
I(P,Q)=\frac{A(P+Q)-A(P)-A(Q)}{2}
\]

when `A` denotes normalized lattice area. Equivalently, one may use Euclidean area without the factor `1/2` in the polarization formula.

`Catalog/Tropical/MixedAreaNormalization.lean` proves the degree-triangle identity, its positive-degree incompatibility with the uncorrected formula, the corrected Bézout identity, symmetry, and additivity in one argument. The explicit `(1,1)` theorem supplies the decisive small-case counterexample computationally inside Lean.

A next step is to define finite lattice polygons and normalized area, prove the full Minkowski polarization law for polygons, and connect that invariant to determinant-weighted stable intersections of balanced fans.

# Future Directions

1. **Additive density.** For every preadditive category `C`, every additive presheaf
   `Cᵒᵖ ⥤+ AddCommGrpCat` is a colimit, in the category of additive functors, of additive
   representables indexed by its category of elements.

2. **Representability from limit preservation.** If `C` is a small finitely complete
   category and a presheaf `F : Cᵒᵖ ⥤ Type` preserves all small limits and satisfies the
   solution-set condition, then `F` is representable.

3. **Sheaf density by represented sheaves.** On every subcanonical site, each type-valued
   sheaf is a colimit in the sheaf category of represented sheaves, with a canonical indexing
   diagram obtained from maps out of represented sheaves.

4. **Classifier uniqueness.** In a category with pullbacks and a terminal object, any two
   subobject classifiers are uniquely isomorphic by an isomorphism commuting with their
   truth arrows.

5. **Predicate extensionality through characteristic maps.** In a category with a subobject
   classifier, two subobjects of `X` are equal precisely when their characteristic morphisms
   `X ⟶ Ω` are equal, and this correspondence is natural under pullback along every
   morphism into `X`.

# Future Directions

Five concrete, falsifiable conjectures arising from the LWE development in
`Catalog/Cryptography/LWE/`. Each is stated so that a single Lean theorem (or a
single counterexample) settles it.

---

## Conjecture 1 (Sharp expansion factor is attained only at the all-ones pattern)

`RingLWEStruct.abs_negaConv_le` proves `‖f ⊛ g‖_∞ ≤ n·‖f‖_∞·‖g‖_∞` in
`ℤ[X]/(Xⁿ+1)`, and the computational evidence shows the bound is attained at
`f = g = (1,…,1)` for `n = 4`.

> **Conjecture.** For every `n ≥ 1` and every `A, B > 0`, the maximum of
> `‖f ⊛ g‖_∞` over `‖f‖_∞ ≤ A`, `‖g‖_∞ ≤ B` equals `n·A·B`, and is attained
> exactly at the sign patterns `f_i = ±A·σ(i)`, `g_j = ±B·σ(j)` with
> `σ(i) = (−1)^{⌊i/1⌋}`-type alternation determined by the target coordinate `k`.

Falsifiable: exhibit `n` and vectors attaining more than `n·A·B` (would refute
the proved bound — impossible), or attaining `n·A·B` at a pattern outside the
predicted family (refutes the "exactly" clause).

**Formal target.** `∃ f g, ∀ k, ... ∧ ∀ f g attaining, pattern` in the style of
`RingLWEStruct.abs_negaConv_le`.

## Conjecture 2 (Optimal-tolerance encodings are exactly the "antipodal" ones)

The original guess here — that the sufficient condition `4|ν| < q` of
`DualRegev.decodeBit_encodeBit_add` is also necessary — has been **refuted**: at
`q = 16` the offset `ν = -4` decodes both bits correctly although `4|ν| = q`,
because the decoding window `[q/4, 3q/4)` is half-open. The correct criterion is
now proved as `DualRegev.decodeBit_correct_iff` (the residue must lie in
`[0, q/4) ∪ [3q/4, q)`), and two further theorems settle the optimality question:
`DualRegev.noise_tolerance_le_half` (no encoder/decoder pair tolerates more than
`q/2` noise residues) and `DualRegev.dualRegev_noise_tolerance_optimal` (the
midpoint encoding attains exactly `q/2`). What remains open is the
*classification* of the optimal pairs.

> **Conjecture.** Fix `q ≥ 2`. An encoder/decoder pair `(enc, dec)` on `ℤ_q`
> attains the maximal tolerance `2·#S = q` **iff** the message gap
> `d = enc(true) − enc(false)` has *even additive order* in `ℤ_q` and the
> correctness region `S` is a transversal of the cosets `{r, r+d}` inside each
> `⟨d⟩`-orbit. In particular, if `d` has odd order `k > 1` then
> `2·#S ≤ q·(k-1)/k < q`, so optimality forces `q` even and, up to relabelling,
> the midpoint encoding.

Falsifiable by an encoder whose gap has odd order yet attains `2·#S = q`.

## Conjecture 3 (Arithmetic form of the arbitrary-modulus regularity criterion)

`LWEReduction.dotHom_surjective_iff_span_top` now proves, for an arbitrary
modulus `q`, that `a ↦ ⟨a, s⟩` is surjective **iff** the coordinates of `s`
generate the unit ideal of `ℤ_q`, and `LWEReduction.dot_fiber_card_general` then
gives exactly `q^{n-1}` preimages per value. What remains open is the purely
arithmetic reformulation of that criterion.

> **Conjecture.** For every modulus `q ≥ 1` and every `s : Fin n → ZMod q`,
> `Ideal.span (Set.range s) = ⊤` **iff**
> `Nat.gcd q (Finset.univ.gcd (fun i => (s i).val)) = 1`.

This is the arbitrary-modulus companion of
`LWEArbModulus.affine_bijective_iff_isUnit`, and would make the regularity
criterion decidable by a single `gcd` computation. The forward direction is a
divisibility argument; the converse needs a Bézout identity for the `gcd` of a
`Finset` of integers, which does not appear to be available directly.

Falsifiable by a composite `q` and a secret whose coordinate `gcd` is coprime to
`q` but which fails to generate `⊤` (or vice versa).

## Conjecture 4 (Ring-LWE noise growth is subgaussian, not worst-case linear)

`RingLWEStruct.rlweResidualNoise_bound` gives the worst-case bound
`n·B_e·B_r + B₂ + n·B_s·B₁` on the LPR decryption noise, and Conjecture 1 says
the factor `n` is attained.

> **Conjecture.** If the coefficient vectors `e, r, s, e₁` are drawn
> independently and uniformly from `{−B,…,B}`, then for every `k` and every
> `t > 0`,
> `Pr[ |(e ⊛ r)_k| ≥ t·B²·√n ] ≤ 2·exp(−t²/2)`,
> so that the *typical* noise growth is `Õ(√n)·B²` rather than `n·B²`, and the
> parameter condition in `rlwe_decrypt_correct` can be relaxed from
> `4(n B_e B_r + B₂ + n B_s B₁) < q` to `4(Õ(√n)(B_e B_r + B_s B₁) + B₂) < q`
> at the cost of an explicit failure probability.

Falsifiable by a distributional simulation exhibiting tails heavier than
subgaussian at scale `B²√n`.

**Formal target.** A Hoeffding/Azuma bound applied to the single-nonzero-entry
row structure established in `RingLWEStruct.abs_twist_row_le`.

## Conjecture 5 (The true optimal smudging distribution)

`LWEReduction.smudging_l1_eq` shows the uniform window of width `N` hides a
shift `c ≤ N` at `ℓ¹` cost exactly `2c/N`. The natural follow-up guess — that
uniform noise is optimal among all distributions supported on `N` consecutive
integers — is **false**: exact rational computation gives, for `N = 3, c = 2`,
`ℓ¹` cost `4/3` for the uniform distribution but `1` for `(1/2, 0, 1/2)`; and for
`N = 8, c = 3`, `3/4` for uniform but `2/3` for `(1/3, 0, 0, 1/3, 0, 0, 1/3, 0)`.
The mechanism: the cost decomposes over residue classes mod `c`, and mass should
be concentrated on the *longest* class.

> **Conjecture.** For all `1 ≤ c ≤ N`, the minimum of
> `∑_x |P(x) − P(x−c)|` over all probability distributions `P` supported on
> `{0, …, N−1}` equals `2 / ⌈N/c⌉`, attained by the distribution that is uniform
> on one residue class `{j, j+c, j+2c, …}` of maximal length and zero elsewhere.
> In particular uniform noise is optimal **iff** `c ∣ N`.

Falsifiable by a distribution beating `2/⌈N/c⌉` for some `(N, c)`.

**Formal target.** Lower bound: total variation along each residue class is at
least twice its maximum, and the class maxima are bounded below by
`mass_j / ⌈N/c⌉`. Upper bound: exhibit the concentrated distribution.

# Tower weights `Wₖ₊₁ = 2^Wₖ · Wₖ`: what is now proved, and what remains

Two self-contained Lean files carry the development:

* `Catalog/Pythagorean/TowerRadix.lean` — the tower weights `W`, the position function `K`,
  the tower radix representation, binary encoding bounds, the iterated logarithm `L₂`,
  the Zeckendorf comparison, and the radix-growth threshold;
* `Catalog/Pythagorean/MixedRadix.lean` — general mixed radix systems (standard and
  balanced), and the balanced tower digits.

Everything below is a theorem in those files unless explicitly flagged as open.  No file
contains `sorry`, and the main results use only Lean's standard axioms.

## Results

### 0. The basic identity

`W k = 2 ^ (∑_{i<k} W i)` (`W_eq_two_pow_sumW`): each tower weight is a power of two whose
exponent is the sum of the previous weights.  Almost every later result rests on this.

### 1. Iterated-log position bound (conjectured, now proved)

With `L₂ n` the number of iterations of `x ↦ ⌈log₂(x+1)⌉` needed to reach a value `≤ 2`:

* `K_le_L2_add_two`: `K n ≤ L₂ n + 2`, via the one-step inequality `K n ≤ K (clg n) + 1`;
* `L2_le_K_add_one`: `L₂ n ≤ K n + 1`, via the auxiliary estimate that everything below
  `2·∑_{i<k} Wᵢ` is killed by `k` iterations;
* `abs_K_sub_L2_le_two`: `|K n − L₂ n| ≤ 2` for **every** `n` (the conjecture asked for
  `n ≥ 2`).

The asymmetric shape is sharp: `K − L₂ = 2` occurs at `n = 2`, and `K − L₂ ≥ −1` always.

### 2. No worst-case binary compression (conjectured, now proved)

* `no_binary_compression`: any encoding injective on `[0, Wₖ)` has a codeword of length at
  least `∑_{i<k} Wᵢ = log₂ Wₖ`.  This is stronger than the conjecture, which only asked
  for prefix-free codes; the reason the stronger form holds is that `Wₖ` is exactly a
  power of two.
* `no_binary_compression_digits`: the same statement phrased for the valid length-`k` digit
  families.
* `blockCode_optimal`: writing digit `i` in exactly `Wᵢ` bits and concatenating gives an
  injective code whose codewords all have length exactly `∑_{i<k} Wᵢ`, so the lower bound
  is attained.

### 3. Radix-growth threshold (conjectured, proved in the following form)

For generalised weights `V₀ = 1`, `Vₖ₊₁ = r(Vₖ)·Vₖ`:

* `genPos_le_L2_add_two`: if `r x ≥ 2^x` for all `x`, then the position function satisfies
  `genPos n ≤ L₂ n + 2`, i.e. it is `O(log* n)`.  Monotonicity of `r`, assumed in the
  informal conjecture, turned out to be unnecessary.
* `sqPos_not_bigO_L2`: for the borderline polynomial radix `r x = x`, i.e.
  `Vₖ = 2^(2^k)`, the position function is *not* `O(L₂)`: for every `c` there is an `n`
  with `c · L₂ n < sqPos n`.

The remaining gap: the negative half is proved for the concrete family `Vₖ = 2^(2^k)`
rather than for every `r` with `r x ≤ x^C`.  The general case should follow from
`Vₖ ≤ V₀^(C^k)` by the same argument, but the bookkeeping with the parameters `C` and
`V₀` has not been carried out.

### 4. Balanced recursive digits (conjectured, now proved)

`MixedRadix` develops mixed radix systems for an arbitrary radix sequence: existence and
uniqueness of digits (`digit_sum`, `digit_unique`), and, for odd radices
`rᵢ = 2sᵢ + 1`, existence and uniqueness of *balanced* digits (`balanced_exists`,
`balanced_unique`).  Specialising to `rᵢ = 2^(Wᵢ+1)+1` gives
`TowerBalanced.balanced_tower_repr`: every integer `x` with `2|x| + 1 ≤ Uₖ` has a unique
length-`k` expansion with `i`-th digit in `[−2^Wᵢ, 2^Wᵢ] = [−(rᵢ−1)/2, (rᵢ−1)/2]`.

### 5. Zeckendorf comparison (partly proved, one clause corrected)

* `Zidx_bounds`: for `n ≥ 1`, `log₂ n + 1 ≤ Z(n) ≤ 2 log₂ n + 3`, with `Z(n)` the largest
  Fibonacci index with `F_{Z(n)} ≤ n` (the top index of the canonical Zeckendorf
  expansion).  This realises the conjectured constants `a`, `b` explicitly as `1` and `2`
  (plus additive slack).
* `K_littleO_Zidx`: `K n = o(Z n)`, in the form: for every `c` there is `N` with
  `c · K n ≤ Z n` for all `n ≥ N`.
* The final clause of the conjecture — that *every injective* binary encoding has
  worst-case length at least `⌈log₂(n+1)⌉` on `[0, n]` — is **false** as stated.
  `injective_code_can_beat_clog` exhibits an injective code of `{0,1,2}` with all
  codewords of length `≤ 1 < 2 = ⌈log₂ 3⌉`.  The correct statement for injective codes is
  `exists_codeword_length_ge`: some codeword has length at least `⌈log₂(n+2)⌉ − 1`.  The
  original bound is recovered exactly when `n + 1` is a power of two — which is the case
  for the tower families, whence conjecture 2 above.

## Open directions suggested by this development

1. **Prefix-free Kraft bound.** Prove the `⌈log₂(n+1)⌉` bound for prefix-free codes on an
   arbitrary interval `[0, n]` (Kraft's inequality is not yet available here).  This would
   restore the last clause of conjecture 5 in its intended form.
2. **General polynomial radices.** Extend `sqPos_not_bigO_L2` from `Vₖ = 2^(2^k)` to every
   monotone `r` with `r x ≤ x^C`.
3. **Exact difference `K − L₂`.** The data suggest `K − L₂ ∈ {−1, 0, 1, 2}` with `2`
   attained only at `n = 2` and `1` only at `n ∈ {1, 3}`.  A complete classification of the
   fibres of `K − L₂` looks within reach of the same techniques.
4. **A balanced analogue of the compression bound.** The balanced tower digits of
   section 4 should admit an optimal fixed-width code as in `blockCode_optimal`, with
   `⌈log₂ rᵢ⌉ = Wᵢ + 1` bits per digit; the small loss `∑ 1 = k` bits relative to the
   information-theoretic optimum would then be exactly quantified.
5. **Zeckendorf-side digit uniqueness.** `Zidx` is defined here as the largest Fibonacci
   index below `n`; formalising the full Zeckendorf expansion (existence and uniqueness of
   the non-consecutive representation) would let the comparison in section 5 be stated
   directly in terms of the expansion rather than its top index.

# Future directions

The thread opened with two questions — the finite-key probability formula and
crossing-probability monotonicity — both of which are proved in
`Catalog/Combinatorics/BernoulliThresholdCoupling.lean`.  Since then the work has
gone into *depth*: a sprinkling/thinning calculus, the Bollobás–Thomason
threshold window, site-dependent densities with the Margulis–Russo formula, a
Poincaré (variance–influence) inequality proved by hybrid paths, its integrated
odds-ratio form, a matching *reverse* Poincaré inequality with the two-sided
Russo differential inequality, and a self-contained `p`-biased Fourier analysis
on the discrete cube.

This cycle completed that Fourier development and used it to convert two of the
inequalities into exact identities:

* `Catalog/Combinatorics/BernoulliFourierParseval.lean` — the product rule for
  the biased expectation, full orthogonality of the characters `ψ_S`, the
  reproducing-kernel identity, **completeness** of the biased Fourier basis
  (`fourier_expansion`), **Parseval** (`parseval`), the biased Plancherel
  identity for Boolean functions (`fourier_weight_sum`), and the exact energy
  decomposition `4P(1-P) = 4p(1-p) ∑_v I_v² + (level ≥ 2 energy)`, which exhibits
  the `ℓ²` influence bound as the statement that a remainder is nonnegative and
  pins down its equality case.
* `Catalog/Combinatorics/BernoulliPoincareDefect.lean` — the identity
  `∑_{S ∋ v} (p(1-p))^{|S|} \hat f(S)² = p(1-p) E[(D_v f)²]` (the biased form of
  `Inf_v(f) = ∑_{S ∋ v} \hat f(S)²`), the resulting Efron–Stein/Poincaré
  inequality **for arbitrary functions** together with its exact defect
  `∑_{S ≠ ∅} (|S| - 1)(p(1-p))^{|S|} \hat f(S)²`, and, for increasing events, the
  Fourier formula for the total influence, the Poincaré inequality with exact
  remainder, and its equality case (`poincare_eq_iff_degree_le_one`).

The following conjectures are the natural next targets; each is falsifiable at
the level of finite site sets, so each can be tested numerically — with the exact
rational harness of `ComputationalEvidence.md` — before being attacked formally.

## Conjecture 1 (two-point hypercontractivity and its tensorization)

For every `f : Bool → ℝ`, every `ρ ∈ [0,1]` with `ρ² ≤ p(1-p)/max(p,1-p)²`, and
the biased noise operator `T_ρ`, one has `‖T_ρ f‖_4 ≤ ‖f‖_2`; and the same
inequality holds for functions on `ι → Bool` with the same `ρ`, by tensorizing
along `expP_prod`.

*The key insight is* that `expP_prod` — proved in this cycle — is exactly the
statement that the biased measure is a product measure, and tensorization of a
hypercontractive estimate is nothing but repeated application of the product
rule coordinate by coordinate; the two-point case is a single two-variable
polynomial inequality accessible to `nlinarith` after clearing denominators.

*Why now?* Hypercontractivity is the only missing ingredient between the present
development and the whole KKL/Talagrand circle: the Fourier expansion, Parseval,
the level decomposition, and the influence identity are all formal already, and
each of them is used verbatim in the classical proof.

## Conjecture 2 (Talagrand's `L¹`–`L²` inequality on the cube)

There is an absolute constant `C > 0` such that for every increasing event `A` on
a finite site set `ι`, writing `I_v = bernProb (1/2) (pivotalSet A v)`,

`P (1 - P) ≤ C · ∑_v I_v / Real.log (Real.exp 1 / I_v)`

(with the convention that a site of zero influence contributes `0`).

*The key insight is* that the present `ℓ²` bound and the defect identity already
give the two extreme cases — the `ℓ²` sum controls the variance exactly, and the
`ℓ¹` sum controls it with the crude Cauchy–Schwarz loss — so Talagrand's
inequality is precisely the interpolation obtained by splitting the Fourier
expansion at the level `log(1/I_v)` and applying Conjecture 1 to the tail.

*Why now?* Talagrand's inequality implies the KKL influence bound
`max_v I_v ≥ c log|ι| / |ι|`, so proving it closes two conjectures of this thread
at once; and its extremal family (tribes) is finite and directly testable
against the rational harness.

## Conjecture 3 (sharp threshold for transitive events)

If the automorphism group of `A ⊆ (ι → Bool)` acts transitively on `ι`, then all
influences are equal, and consequently the width of the density window on which
`bernProb p A` moves from `ε` to `1 - ε` is at most `C(ε) / log |ι|`.

*The key insight is* that under transitivity the Poincaré defect identity forces
`|ι| · I = 4 p(1-p) ∑_v I_v ≥ 4 P(1-P)`, so a *lower* bound on the single common
influence of the KKL type immediately upgrades Russo's formula to a logarithmic
threshold window — the symmetry replaces the union bound entirely.

*Why now?* The equal-influence step is a two-line consequence of the formal
statement `siteEnergy_eq_influence`, since the site energies are manifestly
invariant under automorphisms; only the KKL lower bound (Conjecture 2) is
missing.

## Conjecture 4 (BK / van den Berg–Kesten inequality)

For increasing events `A`, `B` on a finite site set define disjoint occurrence
`A □ B = {η | ∃ S T : Finset ι, Disjoint S T ∧ 1_S ∈ A ∧ 1_T ∈ B ∧ S ∪ T ⊆ open η}`.
Then `bernProb p (A □ B) ≤ bernProb p A * bernProb p B`.

*The key insight is* that `sum_prod_pushforward` already provides the exact
mechanism that BK needs — a coordinatewise duplication of the alphabet from
`Bool` to `Bool × Bool` — so the van den Berg–Kesten induction can be phrased as
a sequence of pushforwards along `Bool × Bool → Bool` rather than as a
measure-theoretic coupling.

*Why now?* The pushforward lemma, the pivotal calculus and the one-coordinate
decomposition `fun_decomp` built in this cycle are exactly the ingredients that
the classical proof manipulates informally; with the thinning law
`bernProb_and_le` already formalized, BK is the last elementary correlation
inequality of percolation still missing from the catalog.

## Conjecture 5 (self-duality of bond crossings at density 1/2)

For bond percolation on the `n × (n+1)` grid, the probability at `p = 1/2` that
the two short sides are joined by an open path equals exactly `1/2`; hence
`thresholdDensity` of that crossing event at level `1/2` is exactly `1/2` for
every `n`.

*The key insight is* that the complement of a horizontal open crossing is a
vertical closed crossing of the dual rectangle, and the map `ω ↦ ωᶜ` is
weight-preserving at `p = 1/2` (`weight (1/2) η = 2 ^ -|ι|` for every `η`), so
the duality is a bijection between two events of equal weight rather than an
analytic statement.

*Why now?* The catalog already has `bondThresholdConfig`, the bond form of the
finite-key formula, and `thresholdDensity`; the missing ingredient is a purely
combinatorial planar-duality lemma between open horizontal paths and closed
vertical paths, which is finite and checkable by enumeration for `n ≤ 3`.

# Future Directions — Exact Piecewise-Linear Partition Bounds for ReLU Networks

The formal development in `Catalog/MachineLearning/ReLUPartition/` establishes,
with 0 sorries and only the standard axioms
(`propext`, `Classical.choice`, `Quot.sound`):

**One layer — the exact maximum.**

* `regionCount_le_schlafli` — one ReLU layer of `n` neurons on `ℝ^d` realises at
  most `∑_{k ≤ d} C(n,k)` activation patterns (Sauer–Shelah route, through a
  Radon-type obstruction giving VC dimension `≤ d`);
* `maximum_regionCount` — that bound is **attained**, by the moment-curve family,
  so `∑_{k ≤ d} C(n,k)` is the exact maximum (`IsGreatest`);
* `vcDim_regions_momentFamily` — the associated set system has VC dimension
  exactly `min n d`;
* `regionCount_recurrence` — a Zaslavsky-style deletion–restriction recurrence.

**Depth — bounds, geometry and an exact example.**

* `card_netRegions_le` — a depth-`L`, width-`w` net on `ℝ^d` has at most
  `(∑_{k ≤ d} C(w,k))^L` cells;
* `convex_netCell` **(new, this cycle)** — every activation cell of a deep ReLU
  network is **convex**, since the cell is exactly the intersection over layers
  of the cells of the affinized single-layer families (`netCell_eq_iInter`);
* `netCell_ordConnected_one` **(new, this cycle)** — in dimension one that
  becomes: every cell is an **interval** of the line;
* `two_pow_le_card_netRegions_sawNet` and `shallow_width_ge_of_matching` — the
  depth-`L` width-two sawtooth has at least `2^L` cells, so a single layer
  matching it needs `≥ 2^L − 1` neurons;
* `card_loudRegions_sawNet` — the sawtooth has precisely `2^L` cells on which no
  layer is silent, one per binary tent itinerary;
* `card_netRegions_sawNet_exact` — the *exact* cell count of the sawtooth
  network,
  ```
    #(sawNet.netRegions L)  =  5 · 2^{L−2} + 1        (L ≥ 2),
  ```
  proved by classifying the degenerate pattern words completely
  (`card_degenRegions_sawNet`: exactly `2^{L−2} + 1` cells have a silent layer),
  with the exact doubling recurrence `card(L+1) = 2·card(L) − 1` and the
  sharpened separation `shallow_width_ge_of_matching_exact` (`5·2^{L−2}` neurons)
  as consequences.

**The sampling gap — the former Conjecture 3, now closed.**

* `abs_sub_sawOrbit_eq` **(new, this cycle)** — an expansion law: two inputs that
  share a *nonsilent* pattern prefix of length `n` have orbits separated by
  exactly the factor `2^n`;
* `sigma_degenerate_singleton` **(new)** — hence every degenerate cell other than
  the two extreme ones is a **single point**: a dying orbit is pinned to `1/2`
  exactly, and the expansion law forbids two preimages;
* `exists_open_interval_loud` **(new)** — conversely every one of the `2^L`
  itineraries is realised on a whole open interval, obtained by pulling an
  interval back through the inverse tent branches;
* `card_openRegions_sawNet` **(new)** — the exact **generic** cell count
  ```
    #(openRegions L)  =  2^L + 2 ,
  ```
  the `2^L` itineraries plus the two unbounded cells `t < 0` and `t > 1`;
* `card_openRegions_lt_card_netRegions` and
  `card_openRegions_eq_card_netRegions_two` **(new)** — the pointwise count
  strictly exceeds the generic one from depth `3` on, but the two **coincide at
  depth 2**; the original conjecture asserted strictness for all `L ≥ 2` and
  needed this correction;
* `tendsto_pointwise_div_open` **(new)** — the ratio of the two counts tends to
  `5/4`: asymptotically a fifth of the pointwise cells is invisible to any
  sampling scheme.

The conjectures below are what the surviving structure and the data in
`ComputationalEvidence.md` point at next.  All are falsifiable by a single
explicit network.

---

## Conjecture 1 (Geometric-sum law in dimension one)

For every width `w ≥ 1` and depth `L ≥ 1`, the maximum number of activation
cells of a depth-`L`, width-`w` ReLU network on `ℝ` is exactly

```
  Σ_{k = 0}^{L} w^k  =  (w^{L+1} − 1) / (w − 1),
```

strictly below the product bound `(w + 1)^L` for `L ≥ 2`.

*The key insight is* that in dimension one a cell is an **interval** — now a
theorem, `netCell_ordConnected_one` — so the cell count of a depth-`l` net is
literally *one more than the number of jump points* of its pattern map.  The
crude recursion `B_{l+1} ≤ (w+1)B_l` (which integrates to the product bound)
counts a fresh zero crossing for every neuron on every interval, but a
pre-activation entering a piece clipped to zero is *constant* there and cannot
cross; charging that loss once per layer gives `B_{l+1} ≤ w·B_l + 1`, which
integrates to the geometric sum.

*Why now?* All three ingredients are formal: `maximum_regionCount` settles the
base case `L = 1` (`w + 1`), `card_netRegions_le` supplies the scaffolding, and
`netCell_ordConnected_one` supplies the interval structure that turns cell
counting into breakpoint counting.  Hand computation at `w = 2, L = 2` already
confirms the predicted value `7` against the product bound `9`, because a sum of
two ReLUs plus a constant is piecewise linear with three pieces whose slopes
cannot alternate in sign.  The exact sawtooth count `5·2^{L−2}+1` sits *strictly
below* the conjectured maximum `2^{L+1} − 1` (`11 < 15` at `L = 3`), so the
sawtooth is **not** extremal: the conjecture predicts a genuinely different
optimiser, a sharp and testable prediction.

*Falsification*: exhibit a width-2 depth-3 network on `ℝ` with `≥ 16` cells.

---

## Conjecture 2 (The `w`-ary sawtooth: exact count for every width)

Let `sawNet_w` be the width-`w` network on `ℝ` whose repeated layer realises the
`w`-fold tent map (the piecewise-linear map with `w` full branches on `[0,1]`).
Then for every `L ≥ 2`

```
  #(sawNet_w.netRegions L)  =  w^L + (w^{L−2} − 1)/(w − 1) + 2,
```

and its *generic* count is exactly `w^L + 2`.

*The key insight is* that our classification of the sawtooth's cells splits into
a *loud* part, counted by the symbolic dynamics of the map (`w^L` itineraries),
and a *degenerate* part, counted by the free prefixes of orbits that fall onto
the fixed point `0`; the second count is a geometric sum in `w` because a
degenerate orbit is pinned two steps before it dies, and only its prefix is free.
The generic half of the prediction is the cleaner one: the pinned cells are
single points for every `w`, by the `w`-ary expansion law.

*Why now?* Both halves are formalised for `w = 2` (`card_loudRegions_sawNet`,
`card_degenRegions_sawNet`, `card_openRegions_sawNet`) and the proofs are written
in terms of the scalar orbit `sawOrbit`, the pinning lemma
`layerPattern_sawNet_eq_empty_iff` and the expansion law `abs_sub_sawOrbit_eq`,
all of which have verbatim `w`-ary analogues; the only genuinely new ingredient
is the `w`-ary version of `exists_itinerary_endpoint`.

*Falsification*: enumerate the cells of the width-3 depth-3 ternary sawtooth; the
conjecture predicts `27 + 1 + 2 = 30` pointwise and `29` generic.

---

## Conjecture 3 (The sampling gap is a general phenomenon)

For *every* ReLU network on `ℝ^d`, the cells invisible to sampling are exactly
those whose affine hull is a proper subspace, and their number is bounded by the
number of full-dimensional cells times a constant depending only on `d`.  For
one-dimensional networks the sharp constant is `1/4`:

```
  #(pointwise cells)  ≤  (5/4) · #(generic cells) ,
```

with equality asymptotically attained by the sawtooth.

*The key insight is* that `convex_netCell` makes every cell a convex set, so
"invisible" is the same as "empty interior", i.e. "contained in a hyperplane";
the sawtooth computation `card_openRegions_sawNet` shows that the extreme case is
driven by orbits that hit a breakpoint exactly, and each such orbit is pinned by
the expansion law, so degenerate cells cannot outnumber generic ones.

*Why now?* The `d = 1` numerator and denominator are both exact theorems this
cycle (`card_netRegions_sawNet_exact`, `card_openRegions_sawNet`), the ratio
statement `tendsto_pointwise_div_open` shows `5/4` is attained in the limit, and
`convex_netCell` gives the general-dimension definition of "generic cell" for
free.  What remains is the inequality itself.

*Falsification*: a one-dimensional network whose pointwise count exceeds `5/4`
times its generic count.

---

## Conjecture 4 (Product bound tight only in the "wide" regime)

The depth-`L` product bound `(∑_{k ≤ d} C(w,k))^L` is attained if and only if
`w ≤ d` — i.e. exactly when a layer can shatter its own neuron set, so that
`∑_{k ≤ d} C(w,k) = 2^w`.

*The key insight is* that the product bound is proved by treating each layer's
pattern as *free* given the previous ones, and freedom is available precisely
when the layer's set system is the full power set; as soon as `d < w` the
Sauer–Shelah deficiency `2^w − ∑_{k ≤ d} C(w,k) > 0` (already formalised as
`schlafli_lt_two_pow`) propagates multiplicatively into a strict loss.

*Why now?* Both halves of the dichotomy have formal handles in place:
`schlafli_eq_two_pow` / `schlafli_lt_two_pow` for the arithmetic, and
`card_netRegions_le` for the bound itself; and the exact sawtooth count gives the
first *quantitative* instance of the failure in the narrow regime
(`d = 1 < 2 = w`, true count `5·2^{L−2}+1` versus product bound `3^L`,
`card_netRegions_sawNet_lt_three_pow`).

*Falsification*: a network with `d < w` attaining `(∑_{k ≤ d} C(w,k))^L` for some
`L ≥ 2`.

---

## Conjecture 5 (Depth hierarchy is strict at every level)

For every `L`, there is a depth-`(L+1)`, width-two network on `ℝ` whose cell
count cannot be matched by any depth-`L` network of width `w ≤ 2^{L/2}`.  In
particular the family of functions computable with `O(L)` cells is a strictly
increasing hierarchy in `L`, not merely in "shallow vs deep".

*The key insight is* that iterating the tent map multiplies the itinerary count
by exactly `2` per layer — a theorem in the sharp form
`card(L+1) = 2·card(L) − 1` — while any depth-`L` network is capped by
Conjecture 1's geometric sum `∑_{k ≤ L} w^k`, so a *single* extra layer already
beats a polynomial widening of the shallower net.

*Why now?* `shallow_width_ge_of_matching_exact` proves the `L` versus `1` case
unconditionally and with the optimal constant `5·2^{L−2}`; upgrading `1` to a
general depth needs precisely the improved upper bound of Conjecture 1, whose
missing structural ingredient (interval cells) is now available as
`netCell_ordConnected_one`.  Conjectures 1 and 5 therefore form a two-step
programme whose first step is a concrete, self-contained recursion lemma.

*Falsification*: a depth-`L` width-`2^{L/2}` network matching the depth-`(L+1)`
sawtooth cell count.

# Future Directions — Sums of Three Cubes

The cycle closed the "local half" of the problem completely: `x³ + y³ + z³ = n` is solvable
modulo every modulus, and has `ℤ_p`-points for every prime `p`, exactly when `n ≢ ±4 (mod 9)`
(`ThreeCubes.locallySolvable_iff`, `ThreeCubes.padicInt_solvable_iff`), `9` is the unique
obstructing modulus (`ThreeCubes.forall_solvableMod_iff`), and the locally solvable integers
have density exactly `7/9` (`ThreeCubes.card_locallySolvable_block`); on the global side the
counting function of representable integers is now bounded below unconditionally by
`repCount N ≫ N^{19/27}` (`ThreeCubes.repCount_ge_nineteen`, sharpening the earlier
`N^{5/9}` of `ThreeCubes.repCount_ge`), and four cubes are shown to cover `162` of the `168`
residue classes modulo `216` that are not `±4 (mod 9)`, in particular every multiple of `3`
(`ThreeCubes.isSumOfFourCubes_of_not_exceptional_216`,
`ThreeCubes.isSumOfFourCubes_of_three_dvd`); only `n ≡ ±38, ±52, ±70 (mod 216)` remain.
What remains is the global half. The five conjectures below are the concrete next steps that
emerged from the analysis and the adversarial review.

---

## Conjecture 1 (Ryley in Lean). Every rational number is a sum of three rational cubes.

**Statement.** `∀ q : ℚ, ∃ x y z : ℚ, x³ + y³ + z³ = q`.

*The key insight is* that the mod `9` obstruction is an artefact of *integrality*, and this
cycle turned that slogan into theorems: `ThreeCubes.rationalCubes_window_1000` shows every
integer with `|n| ≤ 1000` — including all `≡ ±4 (mod 9)` values and all nine integers below
`1000` whose *integral* status is open — is a sum of three rational cubes, and `ThreeCubes.rational_not_integral_infinite` exhibits an infinite family (`5t³`,
`3 ∤ t`) that is rationally but never integrally representable. Moreover
`ThreeCubes.denominator_three_dvd_of_obstructed` proves the denominators of any such
representation must be divisible by `3`, and every witness we found meets that bound exactly
(denominator `3` or `6`).

*Why now?* The reduction is fully in place: by
`ThreeCubes.sum_two_rational_cubes_form`, `q = c³ + a(a²+3b²)/4` is a sum of three rational
cubes for **all** rational `c, a, b`, so Ryley is exactly the surjectivity of the map
`(c,a,b) ↦ c³ + a(a²+3b²)/4`. What is missing is one explicit rational-function section:
a rational point on the quartic `Y² = 3a(4(q-c³) - a³)` uniform in `q`. A symbolic search over
low-degree ansätze is a finite, mechanisable task (the simplest ansatz, denominator `Q = n`
with numerators of degree `≤ 2`, was ruled out by hand: matching coefficients forces
`24s₀² + 12s₁⁴s₀ + s₁⁸ = 0`, whose discriminant `48s₁⁸` is never a rational square), and once
the identity is found the Lean proof is a
`field_simp; ring`. Falsifiable: either the identity checks out for all `q`, or a specific `q`
breaks the candidate identity.

---

## Conjecture 2 (The first open case). `114` is a sum of three integer cubes.

**Statement.** `∃ x y z : ℤ, x³ + y³ + z³ = 114`.

*The key insight is* that this cycle closed the Hasse principle for the entire window
`|n| ≤ 113` (`ThreeCubes.hasse_of_abs_le_113`), so `114` is now literally the first
undecided instance: everything smaller is a theorem, and a single certified triple would push
the verified window forward. Note that `114` is already settled *rationally*:
`114 = (-12)³ + (35/3)³ + (19/3)³` (`ThreeCubes.rationalCubes_open_cases_below_1000`), so the
obstruction to an integral representation — if any — is a genuinely integral phenomenon and
not a local one.

*Why now?* The Lean side is a finished template — a new value costs one line, and the kernel
happily checks `norm_num` identities with 17-digit entries (we already do this for `33`, `42`
and `74`). The mathematical content is entirely a search problem, and the modern
Elsenhans–Jahnel / Booker–Sutherland style algorithm (loop over `d = x + y`, solve the
resulting cubic congruence) is exactly the missing computational ingredient. Falsifiable in
the strong direction: a proof that `114` is *not* a sum of three cubes would refute the Hasse
principle for this surface and would be a major result.

## Conjecture 3 (Positive density of representable integers).

**Statement.** There is `c > 0` such that `#{0 ≤ n < N : n is a sum of three cubes} ≥ cN`
for all large `N`.

*The key insight is* that `ThreeCubes.densitySevenNinths_iff_hasse` shows the *full* `7/9`
density statement is exactly equivalent to the Hasse principle — hence hopeless for now — but
that equivalence also isolates a genuinely weaker and possibly reachable target: any positive
constant `c`. The unconditional record in this development is now
`ThreeCubes.repCount_ge_nineteen`: `16K¹⁹ ≤ repCount (4168K²⁷)`, i.e. `repCount N ≫ N^{19/27}`
(`ThreeCubes.repCount_rpow_ge` states it with a real exponent). It comes from *nesting* the
cube-gap trick over all three cubes: on the boxes `8K⁹ ≤ x < 16K⁹`, `2K⁶ ≤ y < 4K⁶`,
`K⁴ ≤ z < 2K⁴` one has `y³+z³ < (x+1)³-x³` and `z³ < (y+1)³-y³`, so `x = ⌊n^{1/3}⌋`,
`y = ⌊(n-x³)^{1/3}⌋` and then `z` are all recoverable and the parametrisation is injective
(`ThreeCubes.cube_gap_decode`, `ThreeCubes.cube_triple_inj`).  Nesting over `r` cubes gives the
exponent `1 - (2/3)^r`: `5/9` for `r = 2` (the previous bound) and `19/27` for `r = 3`.  Since
`r = 3` is all we have, `19/27` is exactly where the elementary gap method stops.

*Why now?* The gap `19/27 → 1` is now a purely *multiplicative* question: the boxes are as
large as injectivity allows, so any further gain must come from counting values with
multiplicity and subtracting collisions, i.e. from a bound
`#{(x,y,z) : x³+y³+z³ = m, |x|,|y|,|z| ≤ B} = O_ε(B^ε)` for `m ≠ 0` — a divisor-type bound on
the affine surface rather than a Diophantine statement, and one where the counting
infrastructure of this development (`ThreeCubes.repCount`, `ThreeCubes.repCount_mono`,
`ThreeCubes.repsBox`) already applies verbatim. Falsifiable: a proof of `o(N^{19/27})` for the
representable count would contradict the theorem already proved, and a proof of `o(N)` would
refute the conjecture itself.

---

## Conjecture 4 (Exceptionality of `1` and `2` is sharp).

**Statement.** For every `n ∉ {0, 1, 2}` that is not a perfect cube, the number of
representations of `n` of height `≤ B` is `o(B^{1/4})`; equivalently, no `n` outside a thin
exceptional set carries a *polynomial* family of representations.

*The key insight is* that a polynomial one-parameter family
`t ↦ (f(t), g(t), h(t))` with `f³+g³+h³ ≡ n` forces `deg f = deg g = deg h` and a vanishing
leading form `f₀³+g₀³+h₀³ = 0`; by `ThreeCubes.cube_sum_three_eq_zero` (Fermat for exponent
three) one of the leading coefficients must vanish — exactly the mechanism that we already
used to prove `ThreeCubes.containsLine_iff_isCube`. Pushing the same argument from degree `1`
to arbitrary degree should classify all polynomial families.

*Why now?* The degree-one case is fully formalised in this cycle, and Mathlib's
`fermatLastTheoremThree` is the only deep input. The general case needs the same lemma applied
to leading coefficients plus a descent on degree. Falsifiable by exhibiting a polynomial family
for some non-cube `n ≥ 3`.

---

## Conjecture 5 (Four cubes suffice, unconditionally).

**Statement.** `∀ n : ℤ, ∃ a b c d : ℤ, a³ + b³ + c³ + d³ = n`; and, as the concrete next
step, the six residue classes `n ≡ ±38, ±52, ±70 (mod 216)` that this cycle could **not**
cover.

*The key insight is* that a quadruple of *linear* polynomials `xᵢ = aᵢt + bᵢ` has
`∑xᵢ³ = 3(∑aᵢbᵢ²)t + ∑bᵢ³` exactly when `∑aᵢ³ = 0` and `∑aᵢ²bᵢ = 0`, so every solution of
those two equations produces a whole arithmetic progression of sums of four cubes. Searching
that variety gave twelve identities of modulus `18` — e.g.
`(3k-1)³+(3k+1)³+(-3k)³+(-3k)³ = 18k` and `(-9k+2)³+(k+2)³+(6k-1)³+(8k-2)³ = 18k+7` — two of
modulus `54`, and, in this cycle, six more of moduli `72`, `108` and `216`, e.g.
`(-9k+4)³+(k+4)³+(6k-2)³+(8k-4)³ = 72k+56` and
`(-3k+160)³+(-k+71)³+(3k-164)³+(k-35)³ = 216k+92`
(`ThreeCubes.isSumOfFourCubes_of_mod_seventytwo`,
`ThreeCubes.isSumOfFourCubes_of_mod_hundredeight`,
`ThreeCubes.isSumOfFourCubes_of_mod_216_ninetytwo`). Together they cover `162` of the `168`
residue classes modulo `216` with `n ≢ ±4 (mod 9)`
(`ThreeCubes.isSumOfFourCubes_of_not_exceptional_216`), leaving exactly

`n ≡ ±38, ±52, ±70 (mod 216)`.

An exhaustive search of the linear variety over `|aᵢ| ≤ 20`, `|bᵢ| ≤ 50`, and of the
*quadratic* variety `xᵢ = aᵢt²+bᵢt+cᵢ` (five vanishing coefficient conditions) over
`|aᵢ| ≤ 6`, `|bᵢ| ≤ 8`, `|cᵢ| ≤ 10`, produced **no** family whose modulus divides `216` and
whose constant lies in those six classes. That is a sharp, testable sub-conjecture: *no
polynomial family with linear cube-sum meets `±38, ±52, ±70 (mod 216)`.*  The obstruction is
one of method only: the *quadratic* identity
`(x+6s)³ + (x-6s)³ + u³ + u³ = 2(x³+u³) + 216xs²` puts arbitrarily large sums of four cubes in
each of the six classes (`ThreeCubes.exceptional_class_has_arbitrarily_large_four_cube`), e.g.
`648s²+38`, `432s²+70`, `216s²-52`; what it cannot do is fill a class *completely*, because
`s²` runs through a sparse set.

*Why now?* The remaining gap is `6` of the `216` residue classes and is completely explicit.
It can be attacked from either side: enlarge the quadratic (or cubic) search — a finite
computation whose output would be a one-line `ring` identity — or prove the obstruction, which
would have to be a congruence identity linking `3∑aᵢbᵢ²` and `∑bᵢ³` on the variety
`∑aᵢ³ = ∑aᵢ²bᵢ = 0`, and would be a structural theorem of independent interest. Note also
`ThreeCubes.solvableMod_four_cubes`: four cubes have *no* congruence obstruction whatsoever, so
nothing local stands in the way. Falsifiable in both directions.

description:
# Future directions (next cycle)

This cycle closed all five directions carried over from the previous cycle; the
results live in `Catalog/Novelty/EulerMascheroniSharpTails.lean` and are proved
without `sorry`.  Summary of what is now available:

* `gammaTerm_lower_bound` / `gammaTerm_upper_bound`:
  `1/(2(k+2)²) ≤ gammaTerm k ≤ 1/(2(k+1)²)` (rational squeeze of every summand),
  with the sharper `gammaTerm_ge_tele : 1/(2(k+1)(k+2)) ≤ gammaTerm k`.
* `remainder_pos`, `remainder_le_inv_two_mul`:
  `0 < γ − eulerMascheroniSeq n ≤ 1/(2n)` for `n ≥ 1`.
* `tail_lower_sharp`, `tail_upper`, `abs_accelerated_error_le`,
  `accelerated_error_two_sided`: with
  `accelerated n = eulerMascheroniSeq n + 1/(2(n+1))`,
  `1/(14(n+1)²) ≤ γ − accelerated n ≤ 1/(12(n+1)²)` for **every** `n : ℕ`.
* `symKL_eq_sq_div`, `summable_symKL_iff_of_ratio_bounds`,
  `hasSum_symKL_linear_rates`, `not_summable_symKL_geometric_rates`:
  the symmetrized divergence identity, an exact summability criterion for chains
  of positive rates with bounded ratios, and its two test cases.
* `irrational_of_linear_forms`, `irrational_gamma_of_exponential_forms`,
  `accelerated_forms_do_not_decay`: the Apéry-style criterion together with a
  concrete obstruction ruling out the midpoint-accelerated family.

A second file, `Catalog/Novelty/EulerMascheroniEnclosure.lean`, turns the tail
estimate into *effective* arithmetic information about `γ`:

* `eulerMascheroniSeq_fifteen`: `eulerMascheroniSeq 15 = 1195757/360360 − 4 log 2`,
  the approximant at the first index beyond `n = 3, 7` where `log(n+1)` is an exact
  multiple of `log 2`.
* `gamma_gt`, `gamma_lt`: the certified enclosure `0.5771692 < γ < 0.5772158`
  (width `4.66·10⁻⁵`), obtained from `tail_lower_sharp 15` / `tail_upper 15` and
  Mathlib's decimal bounds for `log 2`.  The upper bound is sharp to seven decimals
  because `1/12` is the exact Euler–Maclaurin coefficient.
* `gamma_ne_div_of_den_le`, `gamma_ne_rat_of_den_le`: a finitely checked
  small-denominator obstruction — `γ ≠ p/q` for every `1 ≤ q ≤ 148`.  The threshold
  is optimal for this enclosure since `86/149 = 0.577181…` lies inside the interval.

The engine behind all of it is a family of *derivative-certificate* estimates for
`Λ(z) = log((1+z)/(1-z))` on `[0,1)`:
`2z + 2z³/3 ≤ Λ(z) ≤ min(2z/(1−z²), 2z + 2z³/3 + 2z⁵/(5(1−z²)))`,
each proved by exhibiting the derivative of the difference as an explicitly
nonnegative rational function, then evaluated at `z = 1/(2m+1)`.

Below are the next falsifiable conjectures.

---

## Conjecture 1 (Full Euler–Maclaurin ladder with rational certificates)

For every `j : ℕ` there are explicit rationals `c_1, …, c_j` (the Euler–Maclaurin
coefficients `1/2, 1/12, 0, −1/120, …`) and explicit rational constants
`a_j < b_j` such that

`a_j/(n+1)^{j+1} ≤ (−1)^j (γ − eulerMascheroniSeq n − Σ_{i≤j} c_i/(n+1)^i) ≤ b_j/(n+1)^{j+1}`

for all `n : ℕ`, and the whole ladder can be certified by the single scheme used
here: a `(2j+1)`-term `artanh` truncation for `Λ(z)` at `z = 1/(2m+1)` plus one
polynomial positivity check with positive coefficients after the shift `m = 1+s`.

**The key insight is** that every level of the Euler–Maclaurin expansion of `γ`
reduces, after the substitution `z = 1/(2m+1)`, to positivity of a *single
polynomial with nonnegative coefficients in `m − 1`* — exactly the phenomenon
observed at levels `j = 1` (numerator `2m²+2m+1`) and `j = 2` (numerator
`40(m−1)⁴+240(m−1)³+484(m−1)²+372(m−1)+73`).

**Why now?** The two levels already formalized fix the pattern, the calculus
lemmas are reusable verbatim, and the only new ingredient per level is a
mechanical polynomial-coefficient computation, so the ladder is within reach of
automation rather than requiring new mathematics.

## Conjecture 2 (Optimal constants, and a quadratically growing exclusion threshold)

For the sharp form of the acceleration error, the *best* rational constants are
`γ − accelerated n ∈ [α/(n+1)², 1/(12(n+1)²)]` with
`α = 12·(γ − 1/2) = 0.9265…/12`, i.e. the extreme cases of the two-sided bound
occur at `n = 0` (lower) and in the limit `n → ∞` (upper); equivalently the
sequence `(n+1)²(γ − accelerated n)` is strictly increasing with limit `1/12`.
Consequently, running the `EulerMascheroniEnclosure` argument at `n = 2^j − 1`
(where `log(n+1) = j·log 2` is exact) yields an enclosure of width
`Θ(4^{-j})`, hence excludes all rational denominators up to `c·4^{j}`; the
verified case `j = 4` gives the threshold `148`.

**The key insight is** that monotonicity of `(n+1)²(γ − accelerated n)` should
follow from a *single* per-term inequality of the same telescoping shape used
here, with the comparison sequence `m ↦ 1/(2m) + 1/(12m²) − ε/m³`, and that every
improvement of the pair of constants `(1/14, 1/12)` translates *linearly* into a
larger certified denominator-exclusion threshold.

**Why now?** The `Θ(n⁻²)` statement and the `j = 4` enclosure are both proved; only
monotonicity separates them from the optimal constants, and monotonicity is a
per-term inequality that the existing `logRatio` certificates can likely discharge.

## Conjecture 3 (Symmetrized tails detect exactly the `ℓ²` ratio class)

For any chain of positive rates `a : ℕ → ℝ` whose ratios `ρ n = a(n+1)/a n`
converge to `1`, the symmetrized adjacent divergences are summable **iff**
`(log ρ n)` is square-summable; and the bounded-ratio hypothesis in
`summable_symKL_iff_of_ratio_bounds` can be replaced by `ρ n → 1`.  Moreover the
total symmetrized divergence of the *harmonic* chain `a n = n+1` equals `1`
exactly (proved), while for `a n = (n+1)^p` it equals `p²·ζ(2) + O(p³)` as
`p → 0`.

**The key insight is** that `(ρ−1)²/ρ` and `(log ρ)²` are equivalent
infinitesimals of second order, so summability is a statement about the
`ℓ²`-membership of the logarithmic increments — an information-geometric
restatement of "the chain has finite Fisher length".

**Why now?** The identity `D(a‖b)+D(b‖a) = (a−b)²/(ab)` and the bounded-ratio
criterion are formalized, so only the `ρ → 1` localisation and a comparison
between `(ρ−1)²` and `(log ρ)²` remain.

## Conjecture 4 (No polynomially accurate family can prove irrationality)

Strengthening `accelerated_forms_do_not_decay`: if integer sequences `A n, B n`
with `A n + B n·γ ≠ 0` are built from any approximant family whose error is
`Θ(n^{-d})` for a fixed `d` and whose denominators grow at most polynomially,
then `|A n + B n γ|` is bounded away from `0`; consequently every Apéry-style
attack on `γ` needs approximants with super-polynomial accuracy (e.g.
hypergeometric or Nesterenko-type constructions).

**The key insight is** that the criterion `irrational_of_linear_forms` converts
irrationality into a *rate* statement, and the `Θ(n⁻²)` theorem shows the
classical accelerated harmonic family sits strictly on the wrong side of that
rate threshold.

**Why now?** Both halves — the criterion and a proved two-sided rate for a
concrete family — now exist in the same file, so the general statement can be
attacked by formalizing "polynomial denominators × polynomial error cannot beat
`1/den`".

## Conjecture 5 (Rational-certificate transfer to other Euler-type constants)

The same derivative-certificate scheme (bounds for `Λ(z)` at `z = 1/(2m+1)`,
telescoping comparison, polynomial positivity after the shift `m = 1+s`) yields
sharp two-sided `Θ(n⁻²)` acceleration bounds for the generalized Stieltjes
constants `γ_1` and for `log Γ`-type remainders (Stirling), with all constants
rational and all positivity certificates having nonnegative shifted
coefficients.

**The key insight is** that nothing in the method used `γ` itself: it only used
that the summand is `f(m) − ∫` with `f` a rational function of `m` and the
logarithm entering through `Λ(1/(2m+1))`.

**Why now?** The reusable core (`logRatio_le`, `le_logRatio`, `logRatio_le_pade`,
`hasSum_telescoping`, `hasSum_invSqTele`) is already isolated and general, so a
second constant is mostly a matter of new polynomial certificates.

# Future directions

Derived from the formalization in `Catalog/Pythagorean/SchurIdempotentGammaTwo.lean`, `SchurIdempotentGap.lean`,
`SchurIdempotentAlgebra.lean` and `SchurIdempotentEQCost.lean`.

What is already machine-checked (0 sorries):

* `isBlowUp_iff_gammaTwoLE_one` / `contractive_idempotent_iff_isBlowUp` — a boolean matrix
  has `‖A‖_{γ₂} ≤ 1` iff it is a blow-up of a partial identity matrix (the `L = 1` case of
  the conjecture; Livshits' description of contractive idempotent Schur multipliers).
* `gammaTwoLE_of_signedSum` — the easy direction: a signed sum of `L` blow-ups has
  `‖A‖_{γ₂} ≤ L`.
* `gammaTwoLE_tri2_iff` — `‖[[1,1],[1,0]]‖_{γ₂} = 2√3/3` exactly.
* `gammaTwo_gap` — no boolean matrix has `‖A‖_{γ₂}` strictly between `1` and `2√3/3`.
* `GammaTwoLE.hadamard`, `IsBlowUp.hadamard`, `IsSignedSumOfBlowUps.{add,neg,hadamard,
  complement}` — submultiplicativity and closure of the class of signed sums of blow-ups.
* `eqCost` — the blow-up number, with `‖A‖_{γ₂} ≤ eqCost A ≤ m`, `eqCost A ≤ 1 ↔ A` is a
  blow-up, and `idempotentSchurConjecture_below_gap`: the conjecture holds with `L = 1`,
  uniformly in the matrix size, for every `γ < 2√3/3`.

## Conjecture 1 (second gap). The set of `γ₂`-norms of boolean matrices is discrete near its bottom: after `1` and `2√3/3` the next attained value is `γ₂(T₃)`, where `T₃ = [[1,1,1],[1,1,0],[1,0,0]]`, and no boolean matrix has norm strictly between `2√3/3` and `γ₂(T₃)`.

(Crude numerical searches put `γ₂(T₃)` somewhere in the range `1.40`–`1.48`; the two searches
disagreed, so no numeric value is claimed — pinning it down exactly is part of the
conjecture.)

The key insight is that the gap proof reduces to a *pattern-containment* statement: a boolean
matrix of norm `< 2√3/3` contains no `2`-staircase, and the same forbidden-pattern reduction
should turn "norm `< γ₂(T₃)`" into "contains no `3`-staircase", after which the finitely many
staircase-free structures can be classified exactly as `RowRigid` classifies the
staircase-free case. Why now? The `2`-staircase case is fully formalized here, both the
primal factorization and the dual sum-of-squares certificate; the same two-sided scheme
(explicit `k`-dimensional vector configuration versus an explicit SOS certificate coming from
the dual SDP) transfers verbatim to `T₃`, whose SDP has only six free Gram parameters.

## Conjecture 2 (staircase growth is the only obstruction). For boolean `A`, `‖A‖_{γ₂} ≤ γ` implies that `A` contains no staircase of length `k > 2^{O(γ²)}`, and conversely a boolean matrix with no staircase of length `k` satisfies `‖A‖_{γ₂} ≤ f(k)` for an explicit `f`.

The key insight is that `RowRigid` — the condition characterizing `γ₂ ≤ 1` — is exactly
"no staircase of length `2`", so the whole conjecture on idempotent Schur multipliers may be
a statement about a forbidden-pattern hierarchy rather than about norms. Why now? The `k = 2`
instance is proved in both directions in this project (`isBlowUp_iff_rowRigid` and
`gammaTwo_ge_of_triPattern`), giving a template for the induction, and the "no staircase"
hypothesis is a decidable combinatorial condition that can be tested exhaustively on small
matrices before any proof attempt.

## Conjecture 3 (degree of a boolean matrix). Define `L(A)` as the least number of blow-ups in a signed decomposition. Then `L(A) ≤ 2^{O(γ₂(A)^c)}` with **no** dependence on the matrix size — i.e. the `log*` term in the current best bound is removable — and moreover `L` is submultiplicative: `L(A ⊙ B) ≤ L(A)·L(B)`.

The key insight is that the closure properties proved here (`IsSignedSumOfBlowUps.hadamard`,
`.add`, `.complement`) already give the submultiplicative half for free, so the whole content
is the size-free upper bound, and the natural attack is to bound `L` by the number of
equivalence classes of a rigidity relation defined by *approximate* rather than exact row
equality. Why now? The exact-equality version of that relation is precisely what the
formalized `L = 1` proof uses, and quantitative Cauchy–Schwarz (the same
`∑ (x_i − y_j)² ≤ 0` computation, run with a slack term) turns it into an approximate one.

## Conjecture 4 (arithmetic rigidity of the gap constant). The set `Γ = {‖A‖_{γ₂} : A boolean}` is contained in the field `ℚ(√d : d ∈ ℕ)` — every attained value is an algebraic number of degree `≤ 2` over `ℚ`, and each is attained by a matrix of size polynomial in the degree of the minimal polynomial.

The key insight is that the extremal factorizations arise from semidefinite programs with
rational data whose optimal faces are, in the examples computed so far, one-dimensional,
forcing quadratic irrationalities such as `2√3/3`. Why now? This project produces the first
formally verified exact value of a `γ₂`-norm of a boolean matrix (`2√3/3`), including a
matching primal/dual pair, so the methodology for confirming or refuting further exact values
is in place.

## Conjecture 5 (equality-oracle complexity, effective form). Every boolean matrix with `‖A‖_{γ₂} ≤ γ` is computed by a decision list of at most `poly(γ)` equality queries `f(i) = g(j)`, and this is optimal up to polynomial factors.

The key insight is that a signed sum of `L` blow-ups is literally a `±1`-combination of `L`
equality tests — the formal statement `IsSignedSumOfBlowUps` is already a syntactic
description of an equality-oracle protocol — so the communication-complexity consequence is
an unfolding of the decomposition once the size-free bound of Conjecture 3 is available. Why
now? The translation is formalized (labels are `ℕ`-valued functions of the row and column
index only), so only the quantitative step remains.

# Future directions

Derived from this cycle's results in

* `Catalog/Combinatorics/PrivateAverageDistortion.lean` — the private
  rate–distortion function `D_priv(p) = min_c E_p[d(c,X)]`, its invariance under
  randomization, its exact Hamming value `∑_i min(mass_i(0), mass_i(1))` (majority
  vote), and the uniform value `|α|/2`;
* `Catalog/Combinatorics/RelabelingPrivacy.lean` — orbit distortion under the full
  relabeling group equals the weight gap, the sharp relabeled threshold `⌈|α|/2⌉`,
  the exact orbit (Burnside) ball volume, and the surviving rate converse;
* `Catalog/Combinatorics/PrivacyMeasureConverse.lean` — the measure/Fano-type
  excess-distortion converse `1 − ε ≤ rate · β` and its uniform Hamming form
  `(1−ε)·2^{|α|} ≤ rate · ∑_{i≤D} C(|α|,i)`, with the sharp threshold recovered at
  `ε = 0`;
* `Catalog/Combinatorics/PrivacyTensorization.lean` — additivity of the private
  worst-case distortion across product components.

Each conjecture below is falsifiable and stated so that a single Lean theorem (or a
single explicit counterexample) settles it.

---

## Conjecture 1 (relabeled *average* distortion is a binomial mean deviation)

For the uniform source on `α → Bool` with `n = |α|`, the private **expected**
distortion modulo relabeling is

```
min_c E_unif[ orbDist c X ] = min_{0 ≤ k ≤ n} E[ |k − W| ],   W ~ Bin(n, 1/2),
```

and this minimum equals `n · C(n−1, ⌊(n−1)/2⌋) / 2^{n−1}`, i.e. `Θ(√n)` rather than
`Θ(n)`.

*The key insight is* that the two reductions already proved compose: `orbDist`
depends on its arguments only through the Hamming weight
(`orbDist_eq_dist_wt`), so the average-case private optimization collapses from a
minimization over `2^n` reconstructions to a minimization over `n+1` integers of the
mean absolute deviation of a binomial law — a one-dimensional problem.

*Why now?*  Both halves are in place and formal: the weight reduction is
`orbDist_eq_dist_wt`, and the average-case framework (`privDist`, its `IsLeast`
characterization, and the invariance under randomization) is
`PrivateAverageDistortion.lean`.  What remains is a binomial identity, not a new
information-theoretic idea.  Falsified by any `n` where brute force disagrees.

## Conjecture 2 (marginal determinacy fails for non-additive distortion)

Average-case tensorization is now a theorem: for an *additive* distortion on a
product, `D_priv(p) = ∑_i D_priv(marginal_i(p))` with **no** independence
assumption (`privDist_prodDist`).  The conjecture is that additivity is exactly
what makes this work: for the *max* distortion `d(c,s) = max_i d_i(c_i, s_i)` on a
two-component product,

* the worst-case private threshold is still marginal-determined, namely
  `coveringRadius d = max_i coveringRadius d_i`; but
* the average-case one is **not**: there are two source laws on `σ_1 × σ_2` with
  identical marginals and different `D_priv`, and the gap is bounded by a coupling
  (total-variation) distance between `p` and the product of its marginals.

*The key insight is* that `privDist_prodDist` works only because the expected
distortion of a single reconstruction is linear in the source and additive in the
components, so the optimization decouples; under a `max` distortion the expectation
still is linear but no longer decouples, so joint structure must resurface.

*Why now?*  Both endpoints are formalized: the additive case is closed, and the
covering-radius machinery (`coveringRadius_le_iff`, `exists_far_of_coveringRadius`)
transfers verbatim to a `max` distortion.  A single explicit pair of laws on
`Bool × Bool` settles the second bullet either way.

## Conjecture 3 (entropy form of the measure converse)

Let `p` be a source law on `S`, let a channel with record alphabet `M` have
excess-distortion probability `ε` at radius `D`, and let `β = max_c p(B(c,D))`.
Then

```
H(X) − H(X | Y) ≥ (1 − ε)·(−log β) − h(ε) − ε·log|S|,
```

and the counting statement `mass_good_le_rate_mul_ballMass` is exactly its
`−log`-linearization at `ε = 0`.

*The key insight is* that the fibre decomposition proved here is already the
combinatorial core of Fano's inequality: the fibres of `obs` are the conditioning
events, and the ball-mass bound `β` is precisely the term that becomes `log vol_D`
after taking logarithms.

*Why now?*  The measure version is proved with no measure-theoretic overhead
(finite sums only), so the remaining work is Mathlib's finite-entropy API plus the
concavity of `−x log x`; no new combinatorics is needed.

## Conjecture 4 (partial relabeling interpolates between the two thresholds)

Fix a subgroup `G ≤ Perm α` and let `orbDist_G x y = min_{g ∈ G} hdist(x ∘ g, y)`.
Then the private worst-case distortion `coveringRadius orbDist_G` is a monotone
function of `G` interpolating between `|α|` (for `G = 1`) and `⌈|α|/2⌉` (for
`G = Perm α`), and for `G` acting with orbits of sizes `n_1, …, n_r` on the
coordinates it equals

```
∑_{j=1}^{r} ⌈n_j / 2⌉.
```

*The key insight is* that the invariants of an intransitive coordinate action are
the per-orbit weights, so the covering problem again becomes a product of
one-dimensional interval-covering problems — which is exactly the tensorization
theorem `coveringRadius_prod` applied to the orbit decomposition.

*Why now?*  The two extreme cases are proved (`hamming_coveringRadius` and
`orbit_coveringRadius`) and the additivity machinery needed to glue orbits is
proved (`coveringRadius_prod`); a single lemma identifying `orbDist_G` with a
product distortion would close it.  A subgroup whose value differs from the formula
falsifies it.

## Conjecture 5 (Markov sources give an exponential deficit)

For histories generated by a two-state Markov chain on snapshots with mixing
parameter `δ`, the ambient count `2^{T n²}` in the converse can be replaced by
`2^{T n² · H(δ) + o(T)}`: a private observer at radius `D` must satisfy

```
(1 − ε) · 2^{T n² H(δ)} ≲ ∑_{i ≤ D} C(T n², i),
```

so the privacy threshold drops from `T n²` to `T n² H(δ)` to first order.

*The key insight is* that the measure converse proved here is already stated for an
*arbitrary* source law `p` — only the ball-mass bound `β` changes — so a structured
source enters solely through the maximal ball mass, i.e. through a typical-set
estimate, not through the covering argument.

*Why now?*  `mass_good_le_rate_mul_ballMass` removes the counting restriction that
blocked this direction; what is missing is a typical-set bound on `max_c p(B(c,D))`
for Markov measures, which is a self-contained large-deviation estimate.

---

### Three concrete next-cycle sub-conjectures

1. **(1a)** `min_{0≤k≤n} E|k − Bin(n,1/2)| = n·C(n−1,⌊(n−1)/2⌋)/2^{n−1}` — a purely
   binomial identity, checkable by brute force for `n ≤ 20`.
2. **(4a)** For `G = ⟨(1 2)⟩ ≤ Perm (Fin n)` the relabeled threshold equals
   `1 + (n − 2)`, i.e. only the moved pair contributes a saving.
3. **(3a)** The `ε = 0` case of Conjecture 3: `log rate ≥ log|S| − log vol_D` as a
   statement about `Real.logb`, obtained from `card_le_rate_mul_ball` by taking
   logarithms — the smallest genuinely information-theoretic corollary of the
   present counting results.

# Future directions — strongly complete sets (thread th_20f13f16, cycle 2)

This cycle added two files to the catalog:

* `Catalog/Combinatorics/StronglyCompleteBlocks.lean` — monotonicity, the initial-segment
  criterion (`StronglyComplete A ↔ ∀ k, Complete (A ∩ (k, ∞))`), the **ordered-block
  criterion** `stronglyComplete_of_orderedBlocks`, its dyadic specialization, and the
  sharp negative result `six_per_block_insufficient`.
* `Catalog/Combinatorics/StronglyCompleteResidues.lean` — the **backbone-and-residues
  criterion**, the dilation principle, the refutation of the parity conjecture, the
  necessary congruence condition for strong completeness, and the arithmetic
  characterization `tsum_sqDist_top_iff` of the analytic divergence hypothesis at the
  rational test points `1/d`.

All statements are proved with no `sorry` and no extra axioms.

## What survived, what failed

* **Survived.** Every combinatorial criterion here needs *two* ingredients that are stable
  under finite deletion: a size mechanism (blocks whose subset sums cover long intervals,
  or a backbone representing all large multiples of `d`) and a congruence mechanism
  (infinitely many elements in each residue class). Each of the two alone provably fails:
  `multiplesOfThree` has unbounded size but no residues, `evenWithOne` has a residue but
  only finitely often.
* **Failed as stated.** "Complete + infinitely many odd elements ⟹ strongly complete" is
  false (`complete_infinite_odd_not_stronglyComplete`); parity is only the `d = 2` instance
  of an obstruction that exists for every modulus.
* **Needs a different definition.** A purely combinatorial "six elements per dyadic block"
  criterion cannot exist: `six_per_block_insufficient` produces sets with arbitrarily many
  elements per block that are not even complete. Any such criterion must import a
  hypothesis (analytic or congruential) that excludes subgroup obstructions.

## Conjectures for the next cycle

### C1 (Residue-rich completeness). *If `A` is complete and, for every `m ≥ 2` and every `r`, the class `r mod m` contains infinitely many elements of `A`, then `A` is strongly complete.*

The key insight is that after deleting a finite `F`, the two failure modes are a
*congruence* failure and a *size* failure; residue richness kills the first outright, and
completeness of `A` forces `∑_{a ≤ x, a ∈ A} a ≥ x - O(1)`, a size condition that a finite
deletion changes only by a constant. Why now? This cycle proved the conjecture whenever `A`
carries a `dℕ`-backbone (`stronglyComplete_of_backbone_and_residues`), so only the
backbone-free case remains, and the necessary condition
`infinite_not_dvd_of_stronglyComplete` shows the residue hypothesis is exactly of the right
type. Testable: either extend the backbone argument by replacing "multiples of `d`" with
"subset sums of a tail of `A`", or construct a complete, residue-rich set whose
completeness depends on one small element.

### C2 (Quantitative divergence upgrade). *There is an absolute constant `c > 0` such that: if `A` has at least five elements in every sufficiently large dyadic block and `∑_{a ∈ A} ‖aθ‖² ≥ c · log X` for every non-integral `θ` and every `X` (sum restricted to `a ≤ X`), then `A` is strongly complete.*

The key insight is that the block criterion proved here needs the subset sums of one block
group to cover an interval, and a quantitative divergence bound is exactly what converts
"five well-spread elements per scale" into interval coverage after `O(1)` scales. Why now?
`tsum_sqDist_top_iff` shows that plain divergence only encodes the qualitative statement
"infinitely many elements outside every `dℕ`", which by `six_per_block_insufficient` cannot
suffice on its own; the quantitative form is the first hypothesis strong enough to have a
chance.

### C3 (Deletion depth is unbounded). *For every `k` there is a set `A_k` that stays complete after deleting any `k` elements but fails to be complete after some deletion of `k + 1` elements.*

The key insight is that `threeAndUnits` (deletion depth `1`: deleting `{1,2}` kills it,
deleting either alone does not) should generalize by stacking independent congruence
obstructions modulo distinct primes `p_1 < … < p_{k+1}`. Why now? The refutation machinery
of this cycle (`infinite_not_dvd_of_stronglyComplete` plus explicit witnesses) is exactly
the tool needed, and a positive answer would show that "strongly complete" is not the top
of a finite hierarchy but the limit of a strictly increasing one.

### C4 (Rational divergence is not enough). *There is a set `A` satisfying the rational instances of the divergence hypothesis — `∑_{a ∈ A} ‖a p/q‖² = ∞` for every non-integral rational `p/q` — with six elements in every large dyadic block, which is not complete.*

The key insight is that `tsum_sqDist_top_iff` translates the rational instances into a
purely congruential statement, so a set that is residue-rich but lacunary in size (blocks
of six elements placed at multiplicatively spread positions) should satisfy them while
failing the size requirement. Why now? Such a witness would prove that the *irrational*
test points in the paper's hypothesis are indispensable, delimiting exactly how much of the
analytic input is arithmetic in disguise.

### C5 (Structure of the deletion ideal). *For a complete `A`, the family `I(A) = {F finite : A \ F is not complete}` is upward closed and generated by finitely many minimal elements iff `A` fails only finitely many congruence conditions.*

The key insight is that each minimal `F` should correspond to a modulus `d` for which
`{a ∈ A : d ∤ a}` is finite, so counting minimal obstructions is counting bad moduli. Why
now? `infinite_not_dvd_of_stronglyComplete` gives the easy direction (no bad modulus is
needed for strong completeness), and the dilation principle constructs sets with
prescribed bad moduli, so both directions are within reach of the existing formal API.
