# Future Directions — after the Class-Wide No-Pinning Lemma

The verified core of this cycle (all in `Catalog/Novelty/NoPinning*.lean`, 0 sorries):

* **No-pinning (class-wide).** For a target `N₀` and a candidate `p`, both coprime
  to `L`, infinitely many primes `q` make *every* observable of modulus `L`
  agree on `p·q` and `N₀` (`no_pinning_universal`).  This covers the whole
  poly(log N) battery: residues, Jacobi symbols, gcds (`fullBattery_no_pinning`).
* **The pinned set is exactly the primes dividing `L`** (`compensable_iff_not_dvd`),
  which at level `B` are exactly the primes `≤ B` (`prime_dvd_modLevel_iff`), at
  most `log₂ L` of them (`pinnedPrimes_card_le_log`).
* **Sealing.** Excluding `k` candidates forces `2^k ≤ L`; excluding everything
  below `X` forces `L ≥ 2^(π(X)−2)` (`sealing_bound_semiprime`).
* **No factoring from congruence data**, for arbitrary `L` (`no_congruence_factoring`).
* **Uniformity.** The product map of a group is a perfectly uniform hash:
  every value has exactly `|G|` ordered factorisations (`card_factor_pairs`).

Below are the next-cycle conjectures, each falsifiable and stated so that a
counterexample or a Lean proof would settle it.

---

## Conjecture 1 (Short-interval no-pinning; bold)

*For every even modulus `L`, every target `N₀` coprime to `L` and every prime
candidate `p ∤ L`, there is a compensating prime `q` with `q ≤ L^{C}` for an
absolute constant `C`; consequently the ambiguous partner `N' = p·q` can be
found with the same bit-length as `N₀` up to `O(log L)` bits.*

**The key insight is** that our no-pinning lemma is currently *qualitative in
size*: Dirichlet gives infinitely many partners but no bound, so an adversary
could in principle try to pin a factor using the *size* of `N` in addition to
its residue.  Linnik's theorem already gives `q ≪ L^{5}` unconditionally, so the
conjecture is provable in Lean once an effective Linnik-type input is
formalised; the falsifiable part is the claim that size data adds nothing, i.e.
that one can additionally demand `p·q` to lie in a prescribed dyadic window.

**Why now?** Linnik's constant is now known to be `≤ 5`, and mathlib's Dirichlet
machinery (`Nat.infinite_setOf_prime_and_eq_mod`, Dirichlet characters,
`ZMod` unit groups) is the same infrastructure our proof already uses.

## Conjecture 2 (Beyond congruences: Euler-witness batteries)

*Let `E_a(N) = a^{(N−1)/2} mod N` for `a ≤ B`.  Then for every semiprime target
`N₀` and every candidate prime `p ∤ 2N₀`, there are infinitely many primes `q`
with `E_a(p q) = E_a(N₀)` for all `a ≤ B` — the Euler-witness battery is also
no-pinning.*

**The key insight is** that `E_a(pq)` is determined by `a` modulo the two
Legendre symbols plus a CRT gluing, so the battery is again a function of a
*symmetric* datum of `(p, q)`; the obstruction is that the relevant modulus is
`N` itself, so the compensation must be found in a progression modulo `4·∏a`
together with a prescribed pair of Legendre symbols — precisely the setting our
`IsModObs` framework handles once Legendre data is added as extra coordinates.
Falsified if some `a` makes `E_a` asymmetric in `(p,q)`.

**Why now?** This is the first observable class outside the congruence world
that is still poly(log N)-computable; settling it decides whether "no-pinning"
is a statement about congruences or about poly-time information as such.

## Conjecture 3 (Converse / Ω(N)-sealing, the open half)

*Any observable `f` whose value determines a nontrivial factor of every
semiprime `N ≤ X` — in the sense that some map `A` satisfies `A(f(N)) ∣ N`,
`1 < A(f(N)) < N` — has range of size at least `X^{1/2−o(1)}` on the semiprimes
below `X`.*

**The key insight is** that `no_congruence_factoring` already proves the
qualitative version for congruence observables by exhibiting two coprime
semiprimes with equal readouts; the quantitative version should follow from a
counting argument: each readout value can "serve" only the semiprimes sharing a
prime factor, and there are `~X/log²X` semiprimes but only `~√X/log X` primes,
so a small range forces a collision between coprime semiprimes.

**Why now?** The collision argument needs only elementary counting plus the
prime-counting bounds already in mathlib (`Nat.primesBelow`, Chebyshev-type
estimates), so it is within formalisation reach and would complete the
"factor-revealing ⇒ sealed" half of the programme.

## Conjecture 4 (Entropy form of no-pinning)

*Let `p, q` be independent uniform primes in `[X, 2X]` and let `R = pq mod L`.
Then `I(p ; R) = O(L / X^{1/2})`: the mutual information between a factor and
the congruence readout tends to `0` as `X → ∞` for `L = poly(log X)`.*

**The key insight is** that `card_factor_pairs` already proves the exact
statement "conditioned on the product class, the factor class is uniform"; what
remains is the sampling error between "uniform prime in `[X,2X]`" and "uniform
unit class", i.e. a Siegel–Walfisz input.

**Why now?** Formal information theory (`ProbabilityTheory` entropy API) is
mature enough in mathlib to state `I(p;R)` precisely, and the group-theoretic
half of the argument is already verified here.

## Conjecture 5 (Pinned set characterises the modulus)

*Two even moduli `L₁, L₂` induce the same family of consistent-candidate sets
(for all targets) if and only if `rad(L₁) = rad(L₂)`.*

**The key insight is** that `compensable_iff_not_dvd` shows the consistent set
depends on `L` only through its prime support, so the "if" direction is nearly
proved; the "only if" direction needs a target separating two different radicals,
which the residue channel mod `p` supplies.  This would show that the *only*
invariant of a congruence battery that matters for pinning is its radical — a
strong rigidity statement, and easily falsifiable by exhibiting `L₁, L₂` with
different radicals and identical consistent sets.

**Why now?** All ingredients (`pinned_of_dvd`, `compensable_iff_not_dvd`,
`pinnedPrimes`) are already formalised in this cycle; the remaining work is a
single separating-target construction.

# Future Directions — the cyclic splitting-type channel

Derived from what survived and what failed in this cycle.  Each conjecture is falsifiable by a
single computation on a cyclic order `n`; each is currently supported by exhaustive enumeration
in `ComputationalEvidence.md` but *not* proved.

Notation: for a cyclic Galois order `n`, `T(x) = n / gcd(n, x)` is the splitting type,
`H(T)(n)` its entropy, `nr` the binary "splits completely or not" readout, and
`I_pair(n) = H(Π) − (1/n)Σ_c H(Π_c)` the unordered type-pair / product-residue channel of the
catalog model.

---

## Conjecture 1 (parity dichotomy of the cap)

**For every `n ≥ 2`: `I_pair(n) > 1` if and only if `n` is even and `n ≥ 4`; `I_pair(2) = 1`;
and `I_pair(n) < 1` for every odd `n ≥ 3`.**

*Status.* Proved for prime orders in both directions (`Ipair_prime_lt_one`,
`Ipair_prime_eq_one_iff_two`); verified by exhaustive enumeration for every `2 ≤ n ≤ 24`;
open for general composite `n` (in particular for every odd composite `n ≥ 9`).

*The key insight is* that the cap is a statement about the **2-torsion of the Galois group**,
not about the number of splitting types: the product residue `N ≡ pq` determines the pair type
only through the quotient by squares, so exactly one bit of pair information — the parity bit —
is unconditionally recoverable, and everything above one bit must come from a further even
level of the divisor lattice.

*Why now?* The prime case is now closed in Lean with an exact closed form, so the remaining
content is precisely the composite case; and the coprime additivity of `H(T)`
(`HT_mul_coprime`) plus the Sylow decomposition (`HT_eq_sum_primePow`) give the algebraic
scaffolding that was missing before.

---

## Conjecture 2 (CRT additivity of the pair channel)

**For coprime `m, n > 0`: `I_pair(mn) = I_pair(m) + I_pair(n)`.**

*Status.* The analogous statement for the single-prime channel is a theorem
(`HT_mul_coprime`), and the type map itself is CRT-multiplicative (`typNat_mul_coprime`).
The pair statement is confirmed exactly on all nine tested coprime pairs, including
`I_pair(12) = I_pair(3) + I_pair(4)` and `I_pair(45) = I_pair(9) + I_pair(5)`.

*The key insight is* that the pair channel of `C_{mn}` is the *product channel* of the pair
channels of `C_m` and `C_n`: CRT splits both the type variable and the conditioning residue
into independent coordinates, and mutual information is additive over independent products.

*Why now?* All the ingredients are formalized — the CRT multiplicativity of the type map, the
additivity of `H(T)`, and a general evaluation scheme for `I_pair`.  What is missing is a
product decomposition of the conditional tables `Π_c`, a purely combinatorial step.

Conjecture 1 follows from Conjecture 2 together with the 2-adic law of Conjecture 3 and the
proved bound `I_pair(p) < 1` for odd primes, so this is the highest-leverage target.

---

## Conjecture 3 (the 2-adic pair law)

**For every `k ≥ 1`: `I_pair(2^k) = (4/3)(1 − 4^{−k})`, hence the 2-primary pair channel
saturates at exactly `4/3` bits.**

*Status.* Verified exactly for `k = 1,…,6`.  The corresponding *type* statement is now a
theorem: `H(T)(2^k) = 2 − 2^{1−k}` with `H(T)(2^k) ↑ 2` (`HT_two_pow`,
`HT_two_pow_tendsto`).

*The key insight is* that along the 2-adic tower the conditional pair tables are self-similar:
the table at level `k+1` is the table at level `k` refined by one extra binary square-class
bit, which produces a geometric series with ratio `1/4` — the same self-similarity that gives
the exact type law `2 − 2^{1−k}`.

*Why now?* The type-side geometric law is proved, and its proof (an induction over the divisor
tower `1, 2, …, 2^k` with `φ(2^j) = 2^{j−1}`) is exactly the recursion the pair side needs.

---

## Conjecture 4 (sharp second-order asymptotics of the prime channel)

**`p² · I_pair(p) − log₂ p → 2·log₂ e = 2/ln 2 = 2.885390…` as `p → ∞` along the primes;
in particular `I_pair(p) = (log₂ p + 2 log₂ e + o(1))/p²`.**

*Status.* The two-sided bound `1/(p² log 2) ≤ I_pair(p) ≤ (log₂ p + 5)/p²` is proved
(`Ipair_prime_lower`, `Ipair_prime_upper_sq`); the sharp constant is not.  Evaluating the
proved closed form: `p² I_pair(p) − log₂ p` = 2.7458 (p=5), 2.7838 (p=7), 2.8301 (p=13),
2.8541 (p=23), 2.8782 (p=101), 2.8847 (p=1009) — monotonically approaching `2/ln 2`.

*The key insight is* that in the closed form the `log₂ p` coefficients
`1 − (p−1)(2p−1)/p² + (p−1)(p−2)/p²` cancel to exactly `1/p²`, so the entire remaining channel
is the second-order part of the `log(1 − 1/p)` and `log(1 − 2/p)` expansions, whose `1/p` terms
cancel as well and whose `1/p²` terms combine to `2/ln 2`.

*Why now?* An exact closed form for `I_pair(p)` now exists in Lean, so the asymptotic question
is a pure real-analysis exercise with no combinatorics left in it — a good target for a
Taylor-expansion formalization.

---

## Conjecture 5 (divisor-lattice extremality)

**Among all cyclic orders with exactly `D` divisors, `H(T)(n)` is maximized by the orders whose
type law is closest to uniform on the divisor lattice, and `sup_n (log₂ d(n) − H(T)(n)) = ∞`
while `inf_n (log₂ d(n) − H(T)(n)) = 0` is attained only at `n ≤ 2`.**

*Status.* The upper bound `H(T)(n) ≤ log₂ d(n)` and its strictness for `n ≥ 3` are proved
(`HT_le_logb_card_divisors`, `HT_lt_logb_card_divisors`); the extremal analysis is open.
Numerically the gap is 0.085 at `n = 4`, 0.081 at `n = 6`, 0.36 at `n = 9`, 0.45 at `n = 16`.

*The key insight is* that the deficit `log₂ d(n) − H(T)(n)` is exactly a Kullback–Leibler
divergence between the Euler-φ law `φ(d)/n` and the uniform law on divisors, so the extremal
problem is a KL-minimization over the divisor lattice — a convex problem whose solution should
be dictated by the multiplicities in the prime factorization.

*Why now?* The Gibbs estimate used to prove the bound already exhibits the deficit as a sum of
per-divisor relative-entropy terms, so the KL reformulation is one refactoring away, and the
Sylow decomposition reduces the extremal problem to prime powers.

# FUTURE DIRECTIONS — Singular Moduli Factoring after the √N Theorem

The formalisation in `Catalog/Cryptography/SingularModuli/` settles the basic
question: the gcd-of-class-polynomial-values method is exactly a `√N` method,
its success set has density `≤ 4h/√N`, the class-number speed-up is cancelled by
the evaluation cost, and no precomputed table of evaluation points works for
more than logarithmically many primes. The following conjectures are the natural
next targets. Each is falsifiable, and each is stated so that a counterexample
or a proof would be recognisable in Lean.

---

## Conjecture 1 (Degree–density duality: the barrier is a conservation law)

*For every family of integer polynomials `H_k` with `deg H_k = h_k` and every
family of evaluation strategies, the product (density of useful points) × (cost
of one evaluation) is `O(1/√N)` — the two factors trade off exactly.*

Formally: if `W(H)` denotes any cost measure with `W(H) ≥ deg H` (Horner is
optimal up to constants for a generic polynomial) then
`W(H) · S(H, N) / N ≤ 4·W(H)·h/√N` cannot be improved to `o(1/√N)` by any choice
of `H`, because `S ≤ h(p+q)` is sharp (`successCount_add_two_sq_eq`).

**The key insight is** that `h` appears in the numerator of the density bound
and in the denominator of the per-evaluation cost with the same exponent, so the
`√N` rate is a *conservation law of the construction*, not a limitation of the
counting technique. **Why now?** `total_work_ge` already proves the `√N/4` lower
bound for a single monic `H`; the missing step is a cost model in Lean
(`WorkModel` structure with `W(H) ≥ natDegree H`) and the corresponding
`∀ H, W(H) · N / S(H,N) ≥ √N / 4`, which is a routine generalisation of the
proof already in `Sharpness.lean`.

---

## Conjecture 2 (Elliptic escape: CM torsion evades the counting bound)

*Replacing "evaluate `H_D` at `j₀`" by "compute the `ℓ`-division polynomial of a
random curve `E/ℤ_N` and gcd its value" gives a success density bounded by
`c·ℓ²/√N`, i.e. the same `√N` rate but with `h` replaced by the degree
`(ℓ²−1)/2` — hence still no gain; but the density is achieved for a positive
proportion of curves rather than a proportion `≈ h/p`.*

**The key insight is** that both methods are instances of one scheme: a fixed
integer polynomial whose roots mod `p` encode an arithmetic property of `p`, and
the counting theorem `successCount_eq` applies verbatim, since it never uses
anything about `H_D` beyond its degree. **Why now?** `successCount_eq` and
`successDensity_le` in this repository are already stated for an arbitrary monic
`H ∈ ℤ[X]`, so the whole of ECM-style analysis can be plugged in by instantiating
`H` with division polynomials; only the sharpness direction (existence of roots)
needs new input, namely Hasse's bound.

---

## Conjecture 3 (Adaptive search does not beat uniform search)

*For every adaptive deterministic algorithm that may choose its next evaluation
point as a function of all previously observed gcds, the number of steps needed
to factor a balanced semiprime `N = pq` is at least `√N/(4h)` in the worst case
over `p, q`.*

The results here prove this for *oblivious* (precomputed) strategies
(`finite_family_table_fails`) and bound the *average-case* rate for uniform
sampling (`successDensity_le_balanced`). The adaptive case needs the observation
that a failed trial returns `gcd = 1`, i.e. one bit, so after `k` failures the
adversary's set of consistent `(p,q)` shrinks by at most `k·h(p+q)` residues.

**The key insight is** that a failing gcd query is information-theoretically
almost free for the adversary: it excludes only the `h(p+q)` residues counted by
`successCount_le`, so an adversary argument in the style of
`RandomnessBarrier.arithmetic_trajectory_blind` should give the matching
worst-case bound. **Why now?** The exact criterion (`evalGcd_nontrivialDivisor_iff`)
turns the transcript of an adaptive attack into a purely combinatorial object —
a sequence of residues avoiding two unknown root sets — which is exactly the
setting where a Lean adversary argument is feasible.

---

## Conjecture 4 (Class number cannot be pushed to `√N`)

*For discriminants `|D| ≤ B` the class number satisfies `h(D) = O(√B log B)`,
while the bit size of `H_D` grows like `h(D)^{2+o(1)}`; consequently the
"use a huge class number" strategy has total cost at least `N^{1/2−o(1)}` even
under the most optimistic assumption that a single evaluation costs
`Õ(deg H_D)`.*

**The key insight is** that the barrier proved here is `√N/(4h)` *evaluations*,
so the only way to reach polynomial time is `h ≈ √N`, which forces
`|D| ≳ N/ log² N` and a class polynomial with more than `N^{1/2}` coefficients —
the polynomial itself becomes the exponential object. **Why now?** The Lean
statement needs only the Brauer–Siegel-type upper bound `h(D) = O(√|D| log|D|)`
as an explicit hypothesis; the rest is arithmetic on the bounds already proved,
so the conjecture can be formalised as a conditional theorem today and made
unconditional when Mathlib gains class-number asymptotics.

---

## Conjecture 5 (Universality of the `√N` rung for "algebraic-set" methods)

*Let `f ∈ ℤ[X₁,…,X_m]` be any fixed polynomial and consider the method
"pick `x ∈ (ℤ/N)^m`, output `gcd(f(x), N)`". Then the density of successful `x`
is at most `deg f · (1/p + 1/q)`, so every such method is a `√N` method.*

This is the multivariate generalisation of `successDensity_le`; the substitute
for "at most `deg` roots" is the Schwartz–Zippel bound `#Z(f) ≤ deg f · p^{m−1}`
over `F_p`.

**The key insight is** that the entire barrier rests on one inequality — a
nonzero polynomial has few zeros modulo `p` — so any method whose useful set is
cut out by fixed algebraic equations lands on the same rung, regardless of the
geometry (elliptic curves, abelian surfaces, Drinfeld modules) used to motivate
it. **Why now?** Mathlib has the machinery for Schwartz–Zippel-style counting,
and the CRT transfer lemma proved here (`card_range_filter_crt`) is already
stated for an arbitrary predicate on `ZMod p × ZMod q`, so only the root-count
step needs replacing.

---

### Three concrete next-cycle sub-conjectures

1. **(3a)** Every adaptive strategy making `k` queries factors a uniformly
   random balanced semiprime with probability at most `4kh/√N` (union bound over
   the transcript) — provable from `successCount_le` alone.
2. **(1a)** `successCount H (p*q) = h(p+q) − 2h²` occurs for infinitely many
   primes `p` for each fixed `D` (Chebotarev density for the ring class field),
   making the upper bound attained infinitely often.
3. **(5a)** For `f(X,Y) = Y² − X³ − aX − b` the density of `(x,y)` with
   `gcd(f(x,y), N)` nontrivial is `Θ(1/p + 1/q)`, exhibiting a two-variable
   instance of Conjecture 5 with matching upper and lower bounds.

# Future Directions — Power-Sum GCD Factoring and Carmichael Periodicity

Derived from what survived (and what broke) in the formalisation pass; every item is
stated so that it can be refuted by a single counterexample or closed by a Lean proof.

## What the cycle established (context)

For squarefree `N` and `k > 0`,
`gcd(F(N,k), N) = ∏ { r prime : r ∣ N, (r-1) ∤ k }` (`gcd_powerSum_squarefree`), with the
refinements: the trivial locus is exactly the multiples of `λ(N)`; `λ(N)` is the *minimal*
period; the first informative exponent for a semiprime is exactly `min(p-1,q-1)`; the
read-out is a lattice anti-homomorphism `g_N(gcd(k,k')) = lcm(g_N(k), g_N(k'))`; and the
residue itself is pinned down by the Giuga closed form
`F(N,k) ≡ -∑_{(r-1)∣k} N/r (mod N)`.

**Failure recorded.** The informal claim `p + q = N - λ(N) + 1` is *false* for every
product of two distinct odd primes (`naive_recovery_strict_lt`): the correct identity is
`p + q + λ(N)·gcd(p-1,q-1) = N + 1`. The obstruction, `gcd(p-1,q-1) ≥ 2`, is exactly the
quantity that period-finding does not deliver.

## Conjecture 1 (gcd-lattice reconstruction of the factorisation)

For squarefree `N`, the family `{ gcd(F(N,k), N) : 1 ≤ k ≤ λ(N) }` is closed under `lcm`
and its set of *minimal* nontrivial members is exactly `{ N/r : r prime, r ∣ N }`; hence
the full factorisation of `N` is a lattice-theoretic invariant of the single sequence
`k ↦ gcd(F(N,k),N)`.

*The key insight is* that `g_N` is an order-reversing morphism from the gcd-lattice of
exponents to the divisor lattice of `N` (`gcd_powerSum_gcd_eq_lcm`), so the atoms of the
image lattice must be the co-atoms of the divisor lattice.
*Why now?* The anti-homomorphism law and the product formula are already formalised, so
the conjecture reduces to a finite lattice argument plus a Dirichlet-type statement that
each residue class `r-1 ∣ k`, `(r'-1) ∤ k` is nonempty below `λ(N)`.

## Conjecture 2 (the gcd(p−1,q−1) barrier is intrinsic)

There is no function `Φ` computable in time `polylog(N)` from the pair `(N, λ(N))` alone
that outputs `p + q` for all semiprimes `N = pq`: infinitely many pairs `N ≠ N'` share the
same `(N, λ)` profile modulo the ambiguity `g = gcd(p-1,q-1)`.

*The key insight is* that `λ(N)` determines `(p-1)(q-1)` only up to the factor `g`, and
`g` ranges over an unbounded set as `p, q` vary, so the map `(N, λ) ↦ p+q` is
information-theoretically underdetermined rather than merely hard.
*Why now?* `sum_primes_recovery` isolates `g` as the *only* missing quantity, turning a
vague "period-finding barrier" into a concrete counting question about `g`.

## Conjecture 3 (Giuga/Agoh from the power-sum read-out)

`N > 1` is prime if and only if `F(N,k) ≡ -1 (mod N)` for some (equivalently, every)
`k` divisible by `λ(N)`.

*The key insight is* the closed form `F(N,k) ≡ -∑_{(r-1)∣k} N/r`: when `λ(N) ∣ k` the sum
is `∑_{r ∣ N} N/r`, so the criterion becomes `∑_{r ∣ N} N/r ≡ 1 (mod N)` — precisely
Giuga's condition, which is known to force `N` squarefree and each `r ∣ (N/r - 1)`.
*Why now?* `powerSum_modEq_giuga` and `powerSum_giuga_iff_neg_one` are formalised, so the
open half of the conjecture is now a self-contained statement about Giuga numbers rather
than about power sums.

## Conjecture 4 (sub-quadratic first hit is impossible for the plain search)

For every semiprime `N = pq` with `p < q`, every algorithm that only queries the oracle
`k ↦ gcd(F(N,k), N)` must make at least `min(p-1, q-1)` queries before receiving a value
different from `N`; consequently the plain power-sum search is `Ω(√N)` queries and
`Ω(N^{3/2})` arithmetic operations in the balanced case.

*The key insight is* `gcd_powerSum_eq_self_of_lt_min`: the oracle is *constant* `= N`
below `min(p-1,q-1)`, so no adaptive strategy can extract information there.
*Why now?* The constancy statement is proved; what remains is only the (standard)
adversary argument, which can be formalised as a statement about the query set.

## Conjecture 5 (higher-moment / character generalisation)

For a nontrivial Dirichlet character `χ` mod `m` and squarefree `N` coprime to `m`, the
twisted sum `F_χ(N,k) = ∑_{a=1}^{N} χ(a) a^k` satisfies a product formula in which the
condition `(r-1) ∤ k` is replaced by `χ|_{(Z/r)^*} ≠ (·)^{-k}`, giving a read-out that can
separate primes `r` with the *same* `r-1`.

*The key insight is* that the untwisted proof is nothing but orthogonality of the trivial
character over `(Z/r)^*`; a nontrivial twist replaces the `-1`/`0` dichotomy by a Gauss-sum
dichotomy, adding a second, independent coordinate to the read-out.
*Why now?* The whole untwisted pipeline (block covering, finite-field power sum, CRT
assembly) is formalised and is character-agnostic; only the orthogonality input changes.

# Future directions — carry chains, state, and length generalisation

Derived from the theorems in `Catalog/NumberTheory/CarryChainStatefulCell.lean` and
`Catalog/NumberTheory/CarryChainDepthBound.lean`. Each conjecture is falsifiable: it can
be settled by a Lean proof or by an explicit counterexample construction.

## Conjecture 1 (Sharp state-size threshold: two states suffice and are necessary in every base)

For every base `b ≥ 2`, a cell `C : Cell S` that emits the base-`b` addition digits at
every column induces a surjection from the reachable states onto `Bool` given by the
carry, and conversely a two-element state type suffices; hence `min |S| = 2`,
*independently of `b`*.

*The key insight is* that `cell_must_encode_carry` already shows the carry is a function
of the state, so what remains is reachability of both carry values plus the explicit
`carryCell` witness — the base enters the readout, never the state.

*Why now?* Both halves are in place (`carryCell_correct`, `cell_must_encode_carry`); only
the reachability argument and the packaging as a cardinality statement are missing.

## Conjecture 2 (Depth–radius–length trade-off is tight)

`depth_lower_bound` says a radius-`r`, depth-`d` local circuit correct on all columns
`< n` needs `n ≤ d·r + 1`. Conjecture: this is tight — for every `n`, `r` there is an
explicit circuit of depth `⌈(n-1)/r⌉` computing all digits of `n`-digit base-`b` addition
(prefix-scan over the `Signal` monoid, with `r`-ary composition per layer).

*The key insight is* that `Signal.comp_assoc` makes the carry chain a monoid scan, and a
monoid scan of length `n` with `r`-ary associative combination has depth `⌈log_r n⌉` for
the *balanced* schedule — so the conjecture also predicts that allowing global (not local)
mixing collapses the linear bound to a logarithmic one, isolating *locality*, not depth,
as the operative constraint.

*Why now?* The lower bound is proved; a constructive upper bound would turn the
one-sided wall into an exact complexity characterisation of the task.

## Conjecture 3 (Nontriviality of the carry cohomology class governs the wall)

`carryOf_cocycle` exhibits the carry as a `2`-cocycle of `ℤ/b`. Conjecture: for a general
finite abelian group extension `0 → A → E → Q → 0` with cocycle `c`, a state-free
bounded-window readout can compute the `E`-multiplication of `n` factors *iff* the class
`[c] ∈ H²(Q, A)` is trivial; the carry chain is walled exactly because `[c] ≠ 0` for
`ℤ/b² → ℤ/b`.

*The key insight is* that a coboundary `c = δf` can be absorbed into a per-column
relabelling, which is precisely a state-free position-wise transformation, whereas a
nontrivial class cannot.

*Why now?* The cocycle is already formalised and the state-free failure criterion is
already a theorem, so the two sides can be joined without new machinery.

## Conjecture 4 (Sensitivity dichotomy: the wall is exactly Ω(n) sensitivity)

For a family of "column tasks" `T : (ℕ→ℕ) → (ℕ→ℕ) → ℕ → ℕ` computed by *some* finite-state
cell, the following are equivalent: (i) `T` admits a bounded-window state-free readout;
(ii) the corresponding automaton has trivial (aperiodic, one-state-per-column) Nerode
structure; (iii) `T` has bounded block sensitivity in the sense of
`carry_sensitive_to_lowest_column`.

*The key insight is* that the witness pair used for the carry (differ in one column, flip
every later output) is the generic obstruction: unbounded sensitivity is exactly the
failure mode a fixed receptive field cannot absorb.

*Why now?* All three notions are now available in the same formal vocabulary
(`IsLocalReadout`, `Cell`, `cell_must_encode_carry`).

## Conjecture 5 (Non-commutativity is necessary, not just sufficient)

`no_commutative_pooling_readout` rules out commutative-monoid pooling of *position-blind*
features. Conjecture: it fails as soon as features are allowed to depend on position —
i.e. there is a commutative monoid `M`, a position-dependent `φ : ℕ → ℕ → ℕ → M` and a
decoder computing the carry — but every such construction requires `|M|` to grow with the
number of columns, and `|M| ≥ 2^n` for `n` columns.

*The key insight is* that position-dependent features can serialise the input into a free
commutative structure, so commutativity is only a barrier under a size budget; the
interesting theorem is therefore a *size* lower bound, not an impossibility.

*Why now?* The impossibility for the position-blind case is proved, which pins down
exactly which hypothesis has to be traded for a quantitative bound.

description:
# Future directions: Weil pairings, torsion structure and pairing-based signatures

Derived from what survived, and from what broke, in this cycle.  Each conjecture is
falsifiable inside the framework already built in `Catalog/Cryptography/`:
`AltPairing`, `detPairing`, `weilPairingOfEquiv`, `BLSSetting`.

## What this cycle established (context)

* Bilinearity of a Weil pairing is not merely an axiom: on a group generated by two
  elements, alternation plus bi-additivity *forces* the determinant form
  (`AltPairing.pair_coords`), and on `(ZMod n)²` the nondegenerate alternating pairings
  are exactly the unit multiples of the determinant pairing
  (`altPairing_nondegenerate_iff_isUnit`, `altPairing_symplectic_normal_form`).
* Nondegeneracy is incompatible with cyclic torsion
  (`WeilPairing.torsion_trivial_of_cyclic`).
* Adversarial review killed the previously catalogued BLS model: the axiom
  `Function.Injective (fun P => e(P, G))` in `BLSParams` implies that the whole
  `n`-torsion is trivial (`BLSParams.torsion_trivial`).  The replacement `BLSSetting`
  (two generators, `orderOf e(gen₁,gen₂) = n`) is inhabited (`detBLSSetting`,
  `curveBLSSetting`) and carries the full BLS theory.

## Conjecture 1 (symplectic structure ⇒ square order)

*Every finite abelian group carrying a nondegenerate alternating pairing into a
commutative group has square cardinality, and admits a symplectic basis
`(x₁,y₁,…,x_g,y_g)` with `e(xᵢ,yⱼ) = ζᵢ^{δᵢⱼ}`.*

**The key insight is** that `WeilPairing.torsion_trivial_of_cyclic` is the rank-one case
of a general induction: pick `x` of maximal order, use nondegeneracy to find `y` with
`e(x,y)` of the same order, and split off the orthogonal complement of `⟨x,y⟩`; the
obstruction proved here is exactly the base case that makes the induction start.
**Why now?** The complement step is the only missing ingredient, and Mathlib's theory of
finite abelian groups (`AddCommGroup.equiv_directSum_zmod_of_finite`) supplies the
decomposition to run the induction against.  Falsifiable: exhibit a finite abelian group
of non-square order with a nondegenerate alternating pairing, or fail to close the
induction step for `ZMod p × ZMod p²`.

## Conjecture 2 (Weil pairing from divisors, matching the determinant model)

*The classical divisor-theoretic Weil pairing `e_n(P,Q) = f_P(D_Q)/f_Q(D_P)` on a
Weierstrass curve is, after any isomorphism `E[n] ≅ (ZMod n)²`, equal to a unit multiple
of `detPairing n` — hence `weilPairingOfEquiv` is not merely "a" pairing but "the" Weil
pairing up to a choice of primitive root of unity.*

**The key insight is** that `altPairing_symplectic_normal_form` reduces the identification
to a single computation: any construction that is bi-additive, alternating and
nondegenerate is forced into the determinant normal form, so only the *value on one
basis pair* has to be computed from divisors.
**Why now?** Mathlib has divisors and function fields of curves but no Weil pairing; the
normal-form theorem converts an intimidating identity of rational functions into one
scalar evaluation.  Falsifiable by computing `f_P(D_Q)/f_Q(D_P)` on a small curve (say
`y² = x³ + 1` over `𝔽₇`, `n = 3`) and comparing with `detForm`.

## Conjecture 3 (tight aggregate security is *equivalent* to key registration)

*In the corrected model, aggregate EUF-CMA security holds if and only if public keys are
registered: `aggregate_forgery_extracts` gives the reduction from registration, and
conversely for every unregistered aggregation rule that is a group homomorphism in the
public keys there is a rogue-key forger.*

**The key insight is** that `rogue_key_attack` is not an accident of the sum rule: any
verification equation of the form `e(σ, gen₂) = ∏ e(H_i, pk_i)` is linear in the keys, so
the adversary can always solve for one key that cancels the victim's contribution.
**Why now?** Both halves are already stated in the framework; the converse only needs a
formal definition of "aggregation rule" as a homomorphism and a solvability lemma.
Falsifiable: produce an unregistered, key-homomorphic aggregation rule with no rogue-key
forger.

## Conjecture 4 (pairing-inversion is the exact security boundary)

*In a `BLSSetting`, computing a preimage of the pairing (given `ζ^{ab}` recover
`ab • gen₁`) is polynomial-time equivalent to CDH in `⟨gen₁⟩`, while DDH is trivially
easy (`AltPairing.ddh_iff`); hence the gap-Diffie–Hellman assumption underlying BLS is
exactly "pairing inversion is hard".*

**The key insight is** that the proved equivalence `e(aP,bQ) = e(P,cQ) ↔ ab ≡ c (mod n)`
turns every security question in the group into a question about the single scalar
`orderOf ζ = n`, so the CDH/DDH gap becomes a statement about invertibility of `ζ^·`.
**Why now?** The exponent-level API (`verifies_iff_modEq`, `pair_gen`) already reduces all
BLS statements to congruences mod `n`; a formal cost model is the only missing piece.
Falsifiable by an algorithm that inverts the pairing without solving CDH.

## Conjecture 5 (compression is optimal)

*No verification-equation-preserving encoding of `m` BLS signatures is shorter than one
group element: the aggregation map of `aggregate_compression` is onto the whole group for
every `m ≥ 1`, and any injective-on-verifiable-families encoding needs at least
`log₂ N` bits.*

**The key insight is** the surjectivity half of `aggregate_compression`: since every group
element is a legitimate aggregate, an encoding shorter than `log₂ N` bits must collide on
two aggregates that differ on some verification equation.
**Why now?** The counting statement is already formal; what remains is a pigeonhole
argument relating `Fintype.card` to the codomain of an arbitrary encoding, well inside
current Mathlib.  Falsifiable by a shorter encoding that still decides verification.
title: Derived from what survived, and from what broke, in this cycle.  Each conjecture

description:
# FUTURE DIRECTIONS — NET-47 staircase thread

Four cycles of the loop produced, in `Catalog/NumberTheory/`:

| file | content |
|---|---|
| `KneeStaircaseArithmetic.lean` | binary staircase normal form `stair b j = 2^b(2^j-1)`, digits, 2-adic valuation, injectivity, midpoint law, window classification |
| `KneeStaircaseDivisorSpectrum.lean` | `σ(stair b j)`, abundance criterion, Euclid **and** Euler directions for the family, abundancy monotonicity and its limit |
| `KneeStaircaseOctaveCensus.lean` | exact census of grid-admissible knees in a dyadic octave, count `n - g`, bracket `[(3/4)2^n, 2^n]`, waste ratio `4/3`, renormalisation, the 7/8-median law |
| `KneeStaircaseDivisibilityLattice.lean` | `stair b j ∣ stair b' j' ↔ b ≤ b' ∧ j ∣ j'`, gcd closure, lcm failure, census antichains, grid step recovered as a gcd |
| `KneeStaircaseCensusDensity.lean` | `2·A(n) = n(n+1) + 2` staircase numbers below `2^n`, density `→ 0` |

All statements are proved with no `sorry` and no non-standard axioms.  Below are the conjectures
the cycles left open, each falsifiable and each with a concrete first target.

---

## Conjecture 1 (grid-ratio law). The 7/8 median is a statement about the *sweep grid*, not the network.

**Claim.** For every cell, the seed-averaged knee equals `(1 - 2^{-(r-1)}) · 2^n` where
`2^n` is the product point and `r = n - g` is the grid ratio (`log₂` of product point over grid
step).  In particular a knee distribution with median `≠ (7/8)·2^n` must come from a sweep whose
grid is not `2^{n-3}`.

*The key insight is* that `KneeStaircase.octave_census_card` fixes the number of admissible knees
at `n - g`, and `KneeStaircase.seven_eighths_median_law` shows that for `n - g = 3` the census is
forced to be the arithmetic progression `{(3/4)2^n, (7/8)2^n, 2^n}` whose median is the mean —
so the "7/8 law" is a property of the measuring grid, reproducible with no network at all.

*Why now?*  The round's own next step (a third seed at `ctx = 2048`) tests exactly this: with the
`32`-grid the census is `{192, 224, 256}` (`census_prediction_2048`, proved) and the law predicts
median `224`; with a `16`-grid the census gains `240` and the median must move to `232`.  The
prediction is a single number, decidable by one run.

**First formal target.**  Prove `median (octaveCandidates n g) = 2^n - 2^{g + (r-1)/2}` for odd
`r`, and show the even-`r` census has no member equal to its mean — a *parity obstruction* to any
"mean = median" law when the grid ratio is even.

---

## Conjecture 2 (rigidity of staircase knees). Every knee of a monotone truncation sweep is a staircase number.

**Claim.** If a retention curve `c : ℕ → ℝ` is nondecreasing and its knee is measured on a dyadic
grid, the knee is a staircase number in the sense of `KneeStaircase.IsStaircase`.

*The key insight is* `KneeStaircase.staircase_density_tendsto_zero`: staircase numbers have
density `→ 0` (there are only `n(n+1)/2 + 1` below `2^n`), so the fact that all five measured
knees of the NET series (`16, 32, 64, 96, 112, 128, 224, 256`) are staircase numbers is not
explicable by chance and must come from the geometry of the sweep grid.

*Why now?*  The conjecture is refutable by a single non-staircase knee (e.g. `104 = 1101000₂`,
which is a *sum* of two staircase blocks); refuting it would show the grid, not arithmetic, is
doing the work — and confirming it on a finer grid would make the staircase form a genuine
prediction.

**First formal target.**  Prove that the set of "two-block" numbers (`2^a(2^i-1) + 2^b(2^j-1)`)
has density `→ 0` as well, so that even the weaker "few-block" hypothesis is a strong constraint,
and identify the first grid on which a non-staircase point can win.

---

## Conjecture 3 (antichain obstruction to seed averaging). No knee ensemble admits a common refinement.

**Claim.** For every octave census, the measured knees form a divisibility antichain
(`KneeStaircase.census_antichain`, proved), and consequently no single "law value" `k` can be a
common multiple of two admissible knees while remaining admissible: the family is a
meet-semilattice but not a lattice (`KneeStaircase.staircase_not_lcm_closed`).

*The key insight is* the product order `stair b j ∣ stair b' j' ↔ b ≤ b' ∧ j ∣ j'`: the zero block
must grow while the one block must divide, and along a census the two move in opposite
directions, which is exactly why lcm leaves the family (`lcm 3 7 = 21`).

*Why now?*  The NET series is trying to summarise seed spreads by a single deployable number.
This says any such summary must be an *upper bound* (a join outside the family), never a member —
a structural reason the "guarantee at the conservative end" is the only honest summary.

**First formal target.**  Compute the smallest staircase number above `lcm` of a census (the
"join in the family") and show it equals `2^{n+1}`, i.e. that the only common staircase multiple
of two distinct admissible knees is a full octave up — a factor-2 penalty theorem.

---

## Conjecture 4 (arithmetic type of the knee). Jittered knees are abundant, product points are deficient.

**Claim.** For every cell with grid ratio `r ≥ 2`, all census members except the top point are
abundant, and the top point is deficient; no census member is ever perfect.

Proved here for `2 ≤ j ≤ b` (`KneeStaircase.stair_abundant`), for the top point
(`KneeStaircase.stair_deficient_of_one`), and for weight-7 ladders
(`KneeStaircase.net47_no_knee_perfect`).  The open part is the regime `j > b`, i.e. very fine
grids, where the abundancy ceiling `2σ(2^j-1)/(2^j-1)` of
`KneeStaircase.abundancy_tendsto` can drop below `2`.

*The key insight is* that abundance of `2^b(2^j-1)` is governed by the *ratio* `b : j` and not by
size — the whole family has a `j`-dependent abundancy ceiling, so at fixed `j` the deep rungs are
abundant and at fixed `b` the tall rungs need not be.

*Why now?*  It predicts the exact grid depth at which the arithmetic character of the knee
distribution flips, a discrete, checkable event: the first `(b, j)` with `j > b` and
`σ(2^j-1)(2^{b+1}-1) < 2^{b+1}(2^j-1)`.

**First formal target.**  Prove `stair b j` is deficient whenever `2^j - 1` is prime and `b < j -
1`, closing the classification for prime Mersenne blocks, and exhibit the first composite-block
counterexample.

---

## Conjecture 5 (identifiability of the measurement from the data). The census determines `(n, g)`.

**Claim.** The map `(n, g) ↦ octaveCandidates n g` is injective on `g < n`: the maximum recovers
`2^n` and the gcd recovers `2^g` (`KneeStaircase.census_gcd_is_grid_step`,
`KneeStaircase.net47_gcd_recovers_grid`: `gcd(96,112) = 16`).  Hence a reported knee *set*
carries its own measurement metadata, and any two experiments with the same census used the same
context and the same grid.

*The key insight is* the renormalisation identity `KneeStaircase.census_scaling`: the census is
exactly self-similar under `(n, g) ↦ (n+1, g+1)`, so only the *difference* `n - g` controls the
shape while the pair `(max, gcd)` pins the absolute scale.

*Why now?*  It converts a housekeeping question ("was the sweep grid the same across seeds?")
into a theorem, and it is refuted the moment two cells with different `(n, g)` report identical
knee sets.

**Status.**  The set-level statement is now *proved*: `KneeStaircase.census_determines_params`
shows `(n, g)` is recovered from the census (maximum gives `n`, cardinality gives `n - g`).  What
remains open is the *physical* identifiability: the census sees only the product `n`, never the
pair `(d, ctx)` behind it.

**First formal target.**  Show that the fibre of the census map over a fixed `n` is exactly the
set of cells with `d·ctx = 32·2^n`, i.e. that knee data alone can never separate "depth" from
"context" — a genuine limit on what a truncation sweep can measure, and a prediction that a
`(d = 8, ctx = 512)` cell must report the same census as `(d = 4, ctx = 1024)`.
title: Four cycles of the loop produced, in `Catalog/NumberTheory/`:

description: A vampire number is a composite number v with an even number of digits that can be factizedd as v = x * y where x and y together have the same digits as v. The smallest is 1260 = 21 * 60. But vampire numbers are just the beginning. Define: (1) Werewolf numbers: v = x * y where x and y share exactly one digit with v. (2) Ghost numbers: v = x * y where v has NO digits in common with x or y. (3) Zombie numbers: v = x * y where x and y are both prime (these violate the definition but exist — 125460 = 204 * 615 = 246 * 510, where both factorizations involve a prime and a composite). Conjecture: The density of vampire numbers in [10^{2n}, 10^{2n+1}] approaches 1/sqrt(n) as n -> infinity. Every even-length interval [10^{2k}, 10^{2k+2}] contains at least one vampire number. Ghost numbers have density 0 — they become vanishingly rare as the number of digits increases. Test: enumerate all vampire, werewolf, ghost, and zombie numbers up to 10^8. Prove the density conjecture by counting valid digit permutations. Impact: a playful but genuine number theory of arithmetic creatures — combinatorial digit problems that are easy to state but may be as hard as factoring.
proof_strategy: Define vampire numbers formally: v is a vampire number iff v has 2n digits and there exist x, y each with n digits such that v = x*y and the multiset of digits of v equals the union of digits of x and y. Count the number of digit arrangements: for a 2n-digit number with distinct digits, there are C(2n, n) * n! * n! possible fang pairs, so the expected number of fang pairs is C(2n, n) * (n!)^2 / 10^{2n} = C(2n,n) / 10^n ~ 1/sqrt(n). Prove existence in every interval by constructing explicit vampire numbers using the formula 1260 * 10^{2k} for k >= 0. Test: enumerate up to 10^8.
title: Vampire Numbers and Other Numerical Monsters: A Bestiary of Arithmetic Oddities

description: When a theorem prover searches for a proof, it explores a tree of possible derivation steps. The branching factor is the number of applicable inference rules at each step. Define the proof-search fractal dimension D(T) of a theorem T as the Hausdorff dimension of the set of all successful proof paths for T. If D(T) < 1, the proof is 'easy' (few paths work, so search is focused). If D(T) > 1, the proof is 'hard' (many paths must be explored). Conjecture: For theorems in ZFC, D(T) = 1 + O(1/length(T)). In other words, most theorems have fractal dimension close to 1 — proof search is neither trivially easy nor impossibly hard, but balanced at the edge. Theorems with D(T) << 1 are 'obvious' (direct proofs), and theorems with D(T) >> 1 require exponentially long proofs. The fractal dimension correlates with proof length: if D(T) = 1 + epsilon, then the shortest proof of T has length roughly 1/epsilon. Test: for 1000 theorems in Lean 4's Mathlib, estimate D(T) by Monte Carlo sampling of proof search trees, and correlate with actual proof length. Impact: proof difficulty is a fractal — the dimension of the proof search space determines how hard the theorem is.
proof_strategy: Define the proof search tree for a theorem T: nodes are proof states, edges are inference rule applications, and leaves are states where T is proved or a contradiction is reached. Define the successful path set S(T) as the set of all paths from root to a successful leaf. Define D(T) = dim_H(S(T)) as the Hausdorff dimension. Compute D(T) by box-counting: cover S(T) with boxes of size epsilon and count N(epsilon) boxes. Then D(T) = lim_{epsilon -> 0} log(N(epsilon))/log(1/epsilon). For a balanced binary tree of depth d with 2^d leaves, D = log(2)/log(2) = 1. For a sparse tree with branching factor b < 2, D = log(b)/log(2) < 1. Conjecture: for typical ZFC theorems, the effective branching factor approaches 2 from below, giving D -> 1. Estimate D(T) by MCMC: start from the goal state, randomly apply inference rules, and count the fraction of paths that reach axioms within depth d. D(T) = log(fraction * branching_factor) / log(2). Test: compute for 1000 Mathlib theorems.
title: Fractal Dimension of Proof Search: How Hard Is It to Find a Proof?

description: The logistic map f(x) = r*x*(1-x) for r = 4 exhibits chaotic dynamics: small changes in initial conditions lead to exponentially diverging trajectories (Lyapunov exponent lambda = log(2)). This sensitivity to initial conditions is exactly what a cryptosystem needs. Conjecture: The logistic map at r = 4 is a secure pseudorandom generator. Define the logistic cipher: key = (x_0, n) where x_0 in (0,1) is the seed and n is the number of iterations. The keystream is K = (f^n(x_0), f^{n+1}(x_0), ...) where f^n denotes the n-th iterate. The ciphertext is C = M XOR K where M is the plaintext. The security relies on two properties: (1) Sensitivity: a change of epsilon in x_0 leads to a change of O(1) in f^n(x_0) after n = O(log(1/epsilon)) iterations (exponential sensitivity). (2) Ergodicity: the distribution of f^n(x_0) converges to the invariant measure mu(x) = 1/(pi*sqrt(x*(1-x))) regardless of the initial condition. Conjecture: breaking the logistic cipher (recovering x_0 from K) is as hard as inverting the logistic map, which requires solving a degree-2^n polynomial (since f^n(x) is a polynomial of degree 2^n). This is exponential in n. Test: implement the logistic cipher, measure the period of the keystream (which should be at least 2^n for floating-point precision n), and verify that statistical tests (NIST SP 800-22) pass for n >= 64. Impact: chaos IS cryptography — the logistic map's sensitivity to initial conditions is the same property that makes encryption secure.
proof_strategy: Define the logistic cipher: key = (x_0, n) where x_0 in (0,1), n >= 1. Keystream: K_i = floor(256 * f^{n+i}(x_0)) for i = 0, 1, 2, .... Ciphertext: C_i = M_i XOR K_i. Decryption: compute K from (x_0, n) and XOR again. Security analysis: (1) f^n(x) is a polynomial of degree 2^n in x. Solving f^n(x) = y for x requires finding the roots of a degree-2^n polynomial, which takes O(2^n) time. (2) The Lyapunov exponent lambda = log(2) means that an epsilon error in x_0 propagates to an O(1) error after O(log(1/epsilon)) iterations. For double precision (epsilon = 2^{-52}), this takes about 52 iterations. (3) The invariant measure is the arcsine distribution: mu(x) = 1/(pi*sqrt(x*(1-x))). Keystream bits are approximately uniform. (4) Period: in double precision, the logistic map has a period of at most 2^{52} (due to floating-point representation). In exact arithmetic, the period is infinite. Attack model: given K_0, K_1, ..., K_m, find x_0. This requires solving f^n(x_0) = y_0 where y_0 = K_0/256, which is a degree-2^n polynomial. Test: implement in Python, run NIST SP 800-22 tests for n = 64, 128, 256.
title: Cryptography from Chaos: Encrypting with the Logistic Map

description: The Collatz conjecture (3n+1 problem) states that every positive integer eventually reaches 1 under the map T(n) = n/2 (n even) or 3n+1 (n odd). Despite being verified up to 2^68, a proof remains elusive. Conjecture: the Collatz conjecture is independent of Peano Arithmetic (PA). That is, PA can neither prove nor refute the statement 'for all n, the Collatz sequence starting at n eventually reaches 1'. This would mean the conjecture is TRUE (in the standard model) but UNPROVABLE in PA. The argument: the Collatz map is a Diophantine function that grows faster than any provably total computable function in PA. Specifically, the halting problem for Collatz (does the orbit of n reach 1?) is at least as hard as the consistency of PA, which by Godel's second incompleteness theorem is unprovable in PA. Conjecture: the Collatz conjecture is equivalent to Con(PA) over a weak base theory, meaning that if PA is consistent, then PA does not prove Collatz. Test: formalize the equivalence between Collatz and Con(PA) in Lean 4. Show that a counterexample to Collatz (an n whose orbit diverges or cycles) would imply not-Con(PA). Impact: Collatz might be the simplest true-but-unprovable statement in arithmetic — a concrete example of Godel's incompleteness.
proof_strategy: The argument proceeds in three steps. Step 1: Show that the Collatz halting problem (given n, does T^k(n) = 1 for some k?) is Pi^0_2-complete. This means it is at least as hard as any Pi^0_2 statement, including Con(PA). Step 2: Show that if Collatz is false (there exists n whose orbit diverges or cycles), then Con(PA) implies a contradiction. This would mean not-Collatz implies not-Con(PA), i.e., Collatz follows from Con(PA). Step 3: Show that if Collatz is true, then PA cannot prove it, because the proof would require a consistency-strength beyond PA. The key: the Collatz map can simulate any Turing machine. Specifically, Conway (1972) showed that a generalization of the Collatz map (the 'Fractran' language) is Turing-complete. The specific 3n+1 map is not known to be Turing-complete, but it is conjectured that the set of Collatz orbits encodes the set of PA-proofs. If this is the case, then Collatz is equivalent to Con(PA). Test: formalize the Fractran encoding of Turing machines in Lean 4, show that the 3n+1 map can simulate a register machine, and establish the reduction from Collatz to Con(PA).
title: The Collatz Conjecture Is Undecidable: What If 3n+1 Can't Be Proved?

description: Stone duality states that every Boolean algebra B is isomorphic to the clopen algebra of its Stone space S(B) (the space of ultrafilters on B). This connects syntax (Boolean algebra) with semantics (topology). Conjecture: every neural network f: R^n -> R^m has a 'Stone dual' which is a Boolean algebra B(f) such that the clopen sets of S(B(f)) correspond to the decision regions of f. Specifically, for a binary classifier f: R^n -> {0, 1}, the decision regions {x : f(x) > 0} and {x : f(x) <= 0} are clopen sets in the Stone topology, and the Boolean algebra B(f) is generated by the hyperplanes that form the decision boundary. For a ReLU network with L layers: B(f) is generated by the w_1 + ... + w_L hyperplanes defined by each neuron. The Stone space S(B(f)) has 2^{w_1+...+w_L} points (one for each possible activation pattern), and the decision boundary of f is a subset of S(B(f)). Conjecture: the VC dimension of f equals the number of atoms in B(f), which equals the number of linear regions of f. Test: compute B(f) for small ReLU networks and verify the VC dimension equals the number of linear regions. Impact: neural networks have Stone duals. The Boolean algebra of activation patterns is the syntax, and the decision boundary is the semantics.
proof_strategy: Define B(f) as the Boolean algebra generated by the halfspaces {x : w_i . x + b_i > 0} for each neuron i in the network. An atom of B(f) is a minimal non-empty intersection of these halfspaces and their complements, which is a linear region of f. The Stone space S(B(f)) is the space of ultrafilters on B(f), which has one point for each atom. For a ReLU network with L layers of widths (n, w_1, ..., w_L, 1), the number of atoms (linear regions) is at most prod_{i=1}^{L} sum_{j=0}^{min(n,w_i)} C(w_i, j). The VC dimension of f is at most the number of atoms, since each atom corresponds to a dichotomy that f can realize. More precisely: VC-dim(f) <= log_2(number of atoms), since the number of dichotomies on m points is at most 2^{number of atoms}. Wait, this is the opposite direction. The VC dimension is the largest m such that f can shatter m points, which requires 2^m dichotomies. The number of dichotomies is at most the number of atoms (since each dichotomy corresponds to a subset of atoms). So VC-dim(f) <= log_2(number of atoms). For L = 2, n = 2, w_1 = w: number of atoms <= 2 * C(w, 0) + 2 * C(w, 1) = 2 + 2w. VC-dim(f) <= log_2(2 + 2w). This is much smaller than the known bound O(w * n). So the Stone duality bound is not tight. Conjecture: the Stone duality gives a tighter bound for deep networks. Test: compute B(f) for 2-layer ReLU networks with w = 2, 4, 8, 16, count atoms, compare VC-dim with the bound.
title: Stone Duality for Machine Learning: Neural Networks as Geometric Realizations

Original: Define a natural metric on the space of all mathematical statements and prove that the set of true statements has a fractal dimension. Show that this dimension is strictly between 0 and 1 (truth is sp

description: Hilbert's Hotel has infinitely many rooms, each containing a prime number. Room n contains the n-th prime p_n. The manager can always accommodate a new guest (there are infinitely many primes). But what if the guests want to REARRANGE? Conjecture: For any permutation sigma of N, there exists a rearrangement of the primes q_1, q_2, ... such that the sequence of ratios q_n / p_n converges to 1. In other words, you can shuffle the primes almost arbitrarily and the room numbers barely change. More precisely, the set of permutations sigma for which p_{sigma(n)} / p_n has a limit is dense in the symmetric group (with the topology of pointwise convergence). But NOT every permutation works: the permutation that swaps all even-indexed primes with odd-indexed ones gives q_{2n}/p_{2n} = p_{2n-1}/p_{2n} which converges to 1 by the prime number theorem, but the permutation that reverses order gives q_n/p_n = p_{N-n}/p_n which diverges. Test: compute q_n/p_n for 10 random permutations of the first 10^6 primes and verify that most ratios converge to 1. Find the exact density of 'well-behaved' permutations. Impact: the primes are robust under rearrangement — their asymptotic density is a topological invariant of the permutation group.
proof_strategy: Define a rearrangement of primes as a bijection sigma: N -> N, giving q_n = p_{sigma(n)}. Define a well-behaved rearrangement as one where q_n/p_n -> 1. Prove density: for any epsilon > 0 and any finite partial permutation sigma_0, there exists an extension sigma such that q_n/p_n -> 1. Use the prime number theorem: p_n ~ n*log(n), so q_n/p_n = p_{sigma(n)}/(n*log(n)) = sigma(n)*log(sigma(n))/(n*log(n)). For this to converge to 1, we need sigma(n) ~ n, i.e., sigma must be 'close to the identity' in the sense that sigma(n)/n -> 1. Prove the set of such permutations is dense in Sym(N): for any finite permutation and any neighborhood, extend to a permutation with sigma(n) = n + O(sqrt(n)*log(n)) which satisfies sigma(n)/n -> 1. Prove the reversal fails: sigma(n) = N-n gives sigma(n)/n = (N-n)/n -> infinity. Test: sample 1000 permutations from Sym(10^6) and measure the fraction that are well-behaved.
title: Hilbert's Hotel for Primes: An Infinite Hotel Where Every Guest Is Prime

description: Sorting a list of n elements reduces the entropy from log(n!) bits to 0 bits, doing thermodynamic work W = kT * log(n!) in the process. But this is only true if sorting is irreversible — if the sorted list uniquely determines the input, then sorting is reversible and does no thermodynamic work. The key insight: comparison-based sorting makes irreversible comparisons (you learn a < b but discard the possibility a > b), and each comparison reduces entropy by at most 1 bit. So n*log(n) comparisons reduce entropy by at most n*log(n) bits, which matches log(n!) ~ n*log(n) bits. Conjecture: the minimum thermodynamic work of sorting n elements is W_min = kT * log(n!), and this work is achieved by optimal comparison-based sorting algorithms (merge sort, heapsort). Sub-optimal algorithms (bubble sort: n^2 comparisons) do more thermodynamic work than necessary: W_bubble = kT * n^2, wasting kT * (n^2 - n*log(n)) bits of entropy reduction. Conjecture: any sorting algorithm that makes C(n) comparisons does thermodynamic work proportional to C(n) * kT, and the optimal work is W_min = kT * n*log(n) (Stirling's approximation). Test: simulate sorting algorithms with entropy bookkeeping, verify W = kT * log(n!) for merge sort and W = kT * n^2 for bubble sort. Impact: sorting is a thermodynamic process. The n*log(n) lower bound is a consequence of the second law of thermodynamics.
proof_strategy: Define the entropy of a permutation: S(pi) = -sum_i p_i * log(p_i) where pi is a permutation of n elements. Initially, all n! permutations are equally likely, so S_initial = log(n!) bits. After sorting, only one permutation (the identity) is possible, so S_final = 0. The thermodynamic work is W = kT * (S_initial - S_final) = kT * log(n!). Each comparison in a sorting algorithm reduces entropy by at most 1 bit: comparing a and b tells you one bit (whether a < b or a > b), reducing the number of possible permutations by a factor of at most 2. So C comparisons reduce entropy by at most C bits. For optimal sorting: C(n) = n*log(n) (merge sort), so W = kT * n*log(n) ≈ kT * log(n!) (by Stirling). For bubble sort: C(n) = n^2/2, so W = kT * n^2/2 >> kT * log(n!). The excess work is kT * (n^2/2 - n*log(n)), which is thermodynamic waste. Test: implement merge sort and bubble sort with entropy counters, verify entropy reduction per comparison.
title: The Thermodynamics of Sorting: Entropy and Computational Work

description: A ReLU network f: R -> R with L layers of width w is a piecewise linear function with at most w^L pieces. By the universal approximation theorem, such networks can approximate any continuous function. But HOW WELL can they approximate specific constants? Conjecture: a ReLU network with L layers of width w can approximate pi to within epsilon using O(w * L * log(1/epsilon)) parameters. More precisely, there exists a ReLU network f with L = O(log(log(1/epsilon))) layers and w = O(log(1/epsilon)) width such that |f(1) - pi| < epsilon. This is because pi can be computed by the Leibniz formula pi/4 = 1 - 1/3 + 1/5 - ..., and a ReLU network can implement the partial sums. The number of terms needed is O(1/epsilon), and each term can be computed by a constant-depth ReLU subnetwork. The depth needed is O(log(1/epsilon)) for the sum and O(log(log(1/epsilon))) for the individual terms. Conjecture: the approximation rate for rational numbers by ReLU networks is O(1/(w^L)), matching the piecewise linear structure. For irrational numbers like pi, the rate is O(1/(w * L * 2^L)), which is slower but still exponential in depth. Test: construct ReLU networks that approximate pi, e, and sqrt(2) and measure the approximation error as a function of network size. Impact: ReLU networks approximate constants at a rate determined by their depth and width. Pi requires O(log(log(1/epsilon))) depth.
proof_strategy: Leibniz formula: pi/4 = sum_{k=0}^{infinity} (-1)^k / (2k+1). The partial sum S_n = sum_{k=0}^{n-1} (-1)^k / (2k+1) approximates pi/4 with error O(1/n). To achieve |f(1) - pi| < epsilon, we need n = O(1/epsilon) terms. ReLU implementation: each term t_k = (-1)^k / (2k+1) can be computed as t_k = ReLU(1/(2k+1)) - 2*ReLU(1/(2k+1) - 1/2) (alternating sign). The division 1/(2k+1) requires a ReLU network with O(log(k)) depth (using binary long division). The sum of n terms requires O(log(n)) depth (tree reduction). Total: L = O(log(n) + log(log(n))) = O(log(1/epsilon)) layers. Width: w = O(n) for parallel summation, or w = O(1) for sequential summation with O(n) depth. For the tree reduction: L = O(log(1/epsilon)), w = O(1/epsilon). Better construction: use Machin's formula pi/4 = 4*arctan(1/5) - arctan(1/239), which converges much faster. arctan(1/n) = 1/n - 1/(3n^3) + 1/(5n^5) - ... converges in O(n) terms. For Machin: n terms give error O(1/5^{2n+1}), so only O(log(1/epsilon)) terms needed. Total: L = O(log(log(1/epsilon))), w = O(log(1/epsilon)). Test: implement in Python + Lean 4, measure approximation error vs network size.
title: Diophantine Approximation on Neural Networks: How Well Can ReLU Approximate Pi?

description: The Fibonacci sequence is defined by F(n+1) = F(n) + F(n-1) and converges to the golden ratio. Define the ANTI-Fibonacci sequence: A(n+1) is the smallest positive integer that is NOT equal to A(n) + A(n-1). The sequence begins 1, 1, 2, 4, 7, 11, 16, ... (each term avoids being the sum of the two previous terms). Conjecture: The anti-Fibonacci sequence A(n) grows as A(n) ~ n^2/4, and the ratio A(n)/n^2 converges to 1/4. More precisely, A(n) = floor(n^2/4) + O(1). The sequence avoids the golden ratio entirely — the ratio A(n+1)/A(n) does NOT converge, instead oscillating between 1 and 2. The complement of the anti-Fibonacci sequence (numbers that ARE sums of two previous anti-Fibonacci numbers) has density 0. Test: compute A(n) for n up to 10^6 and verify A(n)/n^2 approaches 1/4. Prove A(n) = floor(n^2/4) + O(1) by induction. Impact: a beautiful counterpoint to the Fibonacci sequence — instead of converging to a constant, it grows quadratically while systematically avoiding addition.
proof_strategy: Define A(1) = A(2) = 1, A(n+1) = smallest positive integer not equal to A(n) + A(n-1). Prove by strong induction: A(n) >= floor(n^2/4). Base: A(1)=1 >= 0, A(2)=1 >= 1. Inductive step: if A(k) >= floor(k^2/4) for k <= n, then A(n) + A(n-1) >= floor(n^2/4) + floor((n-1)^2/4), so A(n+1) <= A(n) + A(n-1) - 1 + delta where delta accounts for gaps, giving A(n+1) >= floor((n+1)^2/4). Prove A(n) <= ceil(n^2/4) + 1 by showing the avoidance constraint only blocks one value per step. Test: compute A(n) for n=1..10^6 and verify A(n)/n^2 -> 1/4.
title: The Anti-Fibonacci Sequence: Numbers That Avoid the Golden Ratio at All Costs

description: The Erdos-Renyi random graph G(n, p) has n vertices where each edge appears independently with probability p. At p = log(n)/n, G(n,p) becomes connected. But what if p is COMPLEX? Define G(n, z) where z is a complex number: each edge (i,j) appears with 'probability' z, meaning the edge weight is z instead of 0 or 1. The resulting 'complex graph' is a weighted complete graph where edge (i,j) has weight z if the edge exists and 0 otherwise. The adjacency matrix A_z has entries that are either z or 0. Conjecture: The complex eigenvalues of A_z trace out a circle of radius |z|*sqrt(n) in the complex plane, centered at the origin. As n -> infinity, the empirical spectral distribution of A_z converges to the circular law (like the Ginibre ensemble) because A_z is a random matrix with i.i.d. entries of mean z*p and variance |z|^2*p*(1-p). The 'hallucination' is that for Im(z) != 0, the graph has complex-valued connectivity — information flows with both amplitude and phase, and the phase creates interference patterns that are visible in the spectral density. Test: generate A_z for n = 1000 with z = 0.5 + 0.3i, compute eigenvalues, and verify they lie in a disk of radius sqrt(n)*|z|. Compare with the Ginibre ensemble prediction. Impact: complex-valued random graphs have circular spectra — the hallucination of complex probabilities creates beautiful circular eigenvalue distributions.
proof_strategy: Define G(n, z) as a random graph on n vertices where each edge (i,j) appears with probability p = Re(z)/|z| if |z| <= 1, or p = 1/|z| if |z| > 1, and the edge weight is z if present and 0 if absent. The resulting matrix A_z has entries A_{ij} = z * B_{ij} where B_{ij} are Bernoulli(p) random variables. The expected value E[A_{ij}] = z*p and Var(A_{ij}) = |z|^2 * p * (1-p). By the circular law for non-Hermitian random matrices (Ginibre, Tao-Vu), the empirical spectral distribution of (A_z - z*p*J)/sqrt(n) converges to the uniform distribution on the unit disk in C, where J is the all-ones matrix. Therefore the eigenvalues of A_z lie in a disk of radius sqrt(n)*|z|*sqrt(p*(1-p)) centered at z*p*(n-1). For z = 0.5 + 0.3i and p = 0.5, the center is at z*0.5*n and the radius is sqrt(n)*|z|*0.5. Test: generate A_z for n = 1000, compute eigenvalues, verify disk shape and center/radius match prediction.
title: Erdos-Renyi on Acid: Random Graphs That Hallucinate

description: Entropy H(X) = -sum p(x) log p(x) measures the information content of a random variable. In category theory, a functor F: C -> D 'loses information' when it maps non-isomorphic objects to isomorphic ones. Define the 'functorial entropy' H(F) as the expected information lost by F: H(F) = -sum_{d in Ob(D)} p(d) * log(p(d)) where p(d) = |F^{-1}(d)| / |Ob(C)|. Conjecture: For the forgetful functor U: Top -> Set that forgets the topology, H(U) = log(2^{aleph_0}) = aleph_0 (infinite entropy, because uncountably many topologies map to the same set). For the abelianization functor Ab: Grp -> AbGrp, H(Ab) = log(2) (each abelian group has 2 non-abelian preimages on average: G and G x Z/2Z). For the inclusion functor Inc: FinGrp -> Grp, H(Inc) = 0 (no information loss, since finite groups embed as themselves). Conjecture: H(F) = 0 iff F is faithful, and H(F) = infinity iff F identifies infinitely many non-isomorphic objects. For finite categories: H(F) = log(|Ob(C)| / |Ob(D)|) when F is 'uniform' (each fiber has the same size). Test: compute H(F) for various functors between finite categories and verify the formula. Impact: entropy is not just a measure-theoretic concept — it is the information-theoretic shadow of functoriality. Every functor loses information, and the entropy measures how much.
proof_strategy: Define functorial entropy: for a functor F: C -> D between finite categories, H(F) = -sum_{d in Ob(D)} (|F^{-1}(d)| / |Ob(C)|) * log(|F^{-1}(d)| / |Ob(C)|). This measures the information lost when F identifies non-isomorphic objects. Properties: (1) H(F) >= 0, with equality iff F is injective on objects up to isomorphism (i.e., F maps non-isomorphic objects to non-isomorphic objects). (2) H(F) is maximized when all fibers have the same size: H(F) = log(|Ob(C)| / |Ob(D)|). (3) H(G circ F) >= H(F) + H(G) for composable functors (subadditivity). (4) For the forgetful functor U: Top -> Set: H(U) = infinity because |F^{-1}(S)| = infinity for every set S with |S| >= 2 (there are uncountably many topologies on S). (5) For abelianization Ab: Grp -> AbGrp: each abelian group A has |F^{-1}(A)| = infinity (there are infinitely many non-abelian groups with abelianization A), so H(Ab) = infinity. Wait, this contradicts the conjecture. Correction: for finite groups, Ab: FinGrp -> FinAbGrp. Each finite abelian group A has finitely many preimages. H(Ab) = log(sum |F^{-1}(A)| / |FinAbGrp|). For small groups: Z/2Z has preimages Z/2Z (abelian) and S_3 (non-abelian with abelianization Z/2Z). Z/3Z has preimages Z/3Z and... (need to enumerate). Test: enumerate all groups of order <= 32, compute their abelianizations, and calculate H(Ab).
title: Categorification of Entropy: The Information Loss of Functors

description: Every real number defines a musical scale: map the digits 0-9 to frequencies f_n = 220 * 2^{n/12} (the A minor pentatonic scale extended). The number pi = 3.14159265... produces the sequence E4, C5, C#5, D5, D#5, F5, E5, A4, G5, C5... — a melody. Conjecture: The melody of pi is not periodic (because pi is irrational) but has musical structure: the autocorrelation of the digit sequence at lag 12 (one octave) is positive and statistically significant. This means pi has more octave-related notes than expected by chance — pi 'favors' notes separated by octaves. Similarly, e 'favors' perfect fifths (lag 7) and sqrt(2) 'favors' minor thirds (lag 3). The musical structure of transcendental numbers reflects their continued fraction properties: numbers with bounded partial quotients have more consonant melodies. Test: compute the digit autocorrelation of pi, e, and sqrt(2) at lags 0-12 (representing unison through octave). Perform a chi-squared test comparing to the uniform distribution. Generate the 'music' of each constant and analyze for tonal centers. Impact: transcendental numbers have musical souls — their digit sequences contain hidden harmonies that reflect their deepest arithmetic properties.
proof_strategy: Map digits 0-9 to frequencies f_n = 220 * 2^{n/12} Hz (chromatic scale starting at A3). Define the melody M(x) for a real number x as the sequence of frequencies corresponding to its decimal digits. Compute the autocorrelation R(k) = sum_{i} (d_i - 4.5)(d_{i+k} - 4.5) / N for lags k = 0,1,...,12. Under the null hypothesis (digits are uniformly random), R(k) ~ Normal(0, 1/N). Test: compute R(k) for pi (first 10^6 digits), e (first 10^6 digits), sqrt(2) (first 10^6 digits). If R(k) > 2/sqrt(N) for some k, that lag is statistically significant. Verify: pi has R(12) > threshold (octave preference), e has R(7) > threshold (fifth preference), sqrt(2) has R(3) > threshold (minor third preference). Connect to continued fractions: bounded partial quotients imply more structure in digit autocorrelations.
title: The Sound of Pi: Musical Structure in Transcendental Constants

description: In the game Werewolf (Mafia), n players include k werewolves and n-k villagers. Each night, the werewolves eliminate one villager. Each day, the villagers vote to eliminate one player (possibly a werewolf). The villagers win if all werewolves are eliminated; the werewolves win if they equal or outnumber villagers. Conjecture: The optimal Bayesian strategy for villagers is to vote for the player with the highest posterior probability of being a werewolf, where the prior is k/n and the likelihood updates are based on the player's voting pattern and survival. More precisely, define the werewolf posterior P(W_i | evidence) using Bayes' theorem: P(W_i) = k/n (prior), P(evidence | W_i) = product of conditional probabilities of observed events given that player i is a werewolf. The optimal strategy maximizes P(villagers win) = P(correct elimination at each day round). For n=7, k=2: the villagers' win probability with optimal Bayesian play is approximately 0.36 (known from game theory). Conjecture: For general n and k, the villagers' win probability is approximately C * (1 - k/(n-k))^2 where C is a constant depending on the information structure. Test: simulate 10^6 games with n=7 to n=20 players and Bayesian villagers, measure the win probability, and fit to the conjectured formula. Impact: social deduction has an optimal Bayesian strategy, and the werewolves' advantage scales as (k/(n-k))^2.
proof_strategy: Define the Bayesian villager strategy: at each day round, each villager computes P(W_i | evidence) for all players i, where evidence includes voting patterns and survival. Update rule: P(W_i | day_vote) proportional to P(day_vote | W_i) * P(W_i). Key likelihood: a werewolf votes to eliminate a villager with probability p_w (strategic) and a villager votes randomly with probability 1/(n-k) for each remaining player. P(villager votes for j | i is werewolf) = p_w * I(j is villager) / (n-k) + (1-p_w) * 1/(n-1). For n=7, k=2: compute optimal p_w by backward induction. The game tree has depth at most 5 (n-k rounds at most). Compute P(villagers win) by Monte Carlo simulation with 10^6 trials. For general n, k: the conjectured formula P(villagers win) = C * (1 - k/(n-k))^2 comes from the observation that each day round eliminates a werewolf with probability k/(n-1) * (1 + information_advantage), so the expected number of werewolves eliminated before all villagers die is (n-k) * k/(n-1) * C'. Simplify to get C * (1 - k/(n-k))^2. Test: verify for n=7 to n=20.
title: Bayesian Werewolf: Optimal Strategy for Social Deduction Games

description: Register allocation in a compiler assigns variables to CPU registers. The interference graph G has variables as vertices and edges between variables that are 'live' at the same time. Register allocation is equivalent to coloring G with k colors (k = number of registers). Conjecture: for SSA-form programs with n variables and maximum interference degree delta, the chromatic number chi(G) satisfies chi(G) = max(delta + 1, omega(G)) where omega(G) is the clique number. This is stronger than Brooks' theorem (which gives chi(G) <= delta + 1) because it predicts that chi(G) = delta + 1 ONLY when G contains a (delta+1)-clique. For typical programs: delta <= 5 and omega(G) <= 4, so chi(G) = delta + 1 <= 6. Conjecture: the optimal number of registers for SSA programs is at most delta + 1, and spill code (storing variables in memory instead of registers) is needed only when k < delta + 1. Moreover, the spill cost is minimized by spilling the vertex with maximum degree in the interference graph (a heuristic known as 'degree-based spilling'). Test: extract interference graphs from 100 real programs, compute chi(G) and delta, and verify chi(G) = max(delta + 1, omega(G)). Impact: register allocation is graph coloring with a precise formula for the chromatic number.
proof_strategy: Interference graph construction: for each variable v in the SSA program, create a vertex. Add edge (u, v) if u and v are live at the same program point. The liveness analysis computes live-in and live-out sets for each basic block. Register allocation = graph coloring of G with k colors. The chromatic number chi(G) is the minimum number of registers needed. Brooks' theorem: chi(G) <= delta(G) + 1, with equality iff G contains a (delta+1)-clique or G is an odd cycle. For program interference graphs: G is typically chordal (no induced cycles of length >= 4), because SSA programs have a tree-like structure. For chordal graphs: chi(G) = omega(G) (the chromatic number equals the clique number). This is because chordal graphs have a perfect elimination ordering, and greedy coloring in this order uses exactly omega(G) colors. Conjecture: SSA interference graphs are chordal. If so, chi(G) = omega(G) = max clique size. The max clique size equals the maximum number of simultaneously live variables, which is delta + 1 (since each variable interferes with at most delta others). So chi(G) = delta + 1 when there is a vertex of degree delta that forms a clique with all its neighbors, and chi(G) < delta + 1 otherwise. Test: extract interference graphs from LLVM IR for 100 programs, compute chordality, chromatic number, and clique number, verify chi(G) = omega(G).
title: The Combinatorics of Compiler Optimization: Register Allocation as Graph Coloring

description:
The single-modulus quantile law of the rescaled residue is now a theorem with an explicit O(1/M) Kolmogorov rate. The conjecture lifts it to a pool of moduli: the pooled law stays within 1/(2 s_min) of the same limit c.d.f., uniformly in the pool composition. It matters because it converts the degeneracy statement into a quantitative budget for every pooled positional test.

For any finite pool of moduli with smallest integer square root s_min, the pooled empirical c.d.f. of v/s^2 on the windows is within Kolmogorov distance 1/(2 s_min) of y -> (sqrt(1+y)-1)/2; hence any pooled positional-versus-magnitude separation statistic is O(1/s_min).

Average the per-modulus bound over the pool in Lean and check numerically on the 128 moduli of exp581 that the pooled deviation stays below 1/(2 s_min).

No pooled experiment at cryptographic scale can separate a positional from a magnitude kernel; positional claims need a different design entirely.

Pool composition creates deviations beyond the per-modulus rate, and cross-modulus mixing is itself a source of apparent structure that must be modelled.
proof_strategy: Convexity: a mixture of c.d.f.s each within epsilon_i of a common limit is within max epsilon_i of it; combine with the proved per-modulus bound.
title: Cross-Modulus Mixture Law for Sieve Window Residues

description:
The fixed-point variety cannot distinguish Rule 110 from Rule 0, but the tower of temporal varieties Per_k does. The conjecture is that the associated dynamical zeta function is rational and separates the Turing-complete rules from the trivial ones, with primitive cycle counts obtained by Moebius inversion over the divisibility lattice already proved in this cycle.

For every n >= 4 the sequences k -> card Per_k(110, n) and k -> card Per_k(0, n) differ, the generating function is rational, and the number of primitive k-cycles of Rule 110 is positive for infinitely many pairs (n, k).

Define primitiveCycleCount by Moebius inversion using periodicSet_inter, prove positivity for Rule 110 at n = 4, 8, 12 by kernel-checked decision, and prove the Rule 0 tower collapses using rule0_periodicSet.

A computable, algebraically defined invariant that tracks class-4 behaviour where the fixed-point variety is provably blind.

Periodic-orbit counts are also class-blind, forcing the search for invariants into space-time or ideal-theoretic data.
proof_strategy: Moebius inversion over the divisor lattice, using periodicSet_inter and step_bijOn_periodicSet to justify that each level is a disjoint union of cycles.
title: Zeta-Function Separation of Universality Classes

description:
The Bell basis proved here is a unitary error basis: an orthonormal basis of the matrix space whose members are multiples of unitaries. Conjecture that in dimension two every such basis is the Pauli basis up to phases and a global unitary, a rigidity statement of the same combinatorial flavour as Hadamard equivalence.

If B : Fin 4 → Matrix (Fin 2) (Fin 2) ℂ is orthonormal for the Hilbert–Schmidt inner product and each √2·B k is unitary, then there are phases c k and unitaries U, V with B k = c k • (U * pauliMat (σ k) * V) for some permutation σ.

Formalize by expanding each B k in the Pauli basis (bellBasis_expansion gives the expansion map), translating unitarity into a norm condition on the coefficient vectors, and classifying the resulting orthogonal 4 × 4 coefficient matrices.

Dimension two has a unique unitary error basis up to equivalence, giving a verified anchor for the general nice-error-basis classification used in quantum error correction.

An exotic order-two error basis would exist, which would be a genuinely new combinatorial design and would refute folklore uniqueness.
